We can now refine our question.

Question 1.2.4.18.

Can we recover any spectrum X from its p-completions Xp∧ as p ranges over all primes together with its rationalization Xℚ?

Our slogan will be that the answer to this question is yes if we also include the data of a certain “gluing map.” This uses something known as the Hasse square.

For every spectrum we have maps

X→Xp∧andX→Xℚ.

In addition, rationalizing the p-completion map, we have maps

Xℚ→(Xp∧)ℚ≕Xℚp.

By naturality properties of rationalization, we obtain a commutative square

This is called the Hasse square or the fracture square.

Theorem 1.2.4.19.

For any spectrum X, this square is a fiber product.

This theorem is proved by noting that p is invertible on the fiber of X→Xp∧. Therefore, the fiber of the top row is rational (because all primes are invertible), so it equals its rationalization, which is the fiber of the bottom row.

The theorem can be refined to the categorical level. In particular, we have a pullback diagram

of ∞-categories. This means that we can decompose the entire ∞-category of spectra.

Unfortunately, this morphism is not symmetric monoidal, but it at least behaves well with respect to 𝔼n-algebras. More precisely, there is a pullback square

of ∞-categories, where the arrows are given by restriction from the previous square.

1.2.5 Tate construction

Let G be a group object in 𝒮. In particular, this means that G is a group-like 𝔼1-space. These can in fact be modeled by topological groups, but the correct generality is that of group-like 𝔼1-spaces. There is a classifying space B⁢G∈𝒮 given by the bar construction. If 𝒞 is any ∞-category, we will let

𝒞B⁢G=𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢G,𝒞)

denote the category of objects in 𝒞 with a G-action.

Construction 1.2.5.1.

We will consider G as an object in 𝒮G×G by letting G×G act on G by the action

(g,h)⋅h≔g⁢x⁢h−1.
Definition 1.2.5.2 (Klein).

We define a spectrum DG∈𝖲𝗉B⁢G called the dualizing spectrum of G as

DG≔(Σ+∞⁢G)h⁡(G×1)

with its remaining G=1×G-action.

The name dualizing spectrum needs a justification, which will be given in the remainder of this section. Before we do this, we give some examples.

Example 1.2.5.3.

Assume G is a finite group. Then

Σ+∞⁢G=⨁g∈G𝕊.

Computing the homotopy fixed points, we obtain

(Σ+∞⁢G)h⁢G=(⨁g∈G𝕊)h⁢G≃𝕊.

More precisely, the map

(⨁g∈G𝕊)h⁢G→⨁g∈G𝕊→𝕊

is an equivalence.

To see this, consider the homotopy fixed point spectral sequence

H∗⁢(G,⨁g∈Gπ∗⁢𝕊)⟹π∗⁢((⨁g∈G𝕊)h⁢G).

It is a classical result that

H∗⁢(G,⨁g∈GA)={A∗=00∗≠0.

Therefore the spectral sequence degenerates and yields the result. This implies that DG=𝕊 with the trivial action.

Now suppose that G is a compact Lie group.

Theorem 1.2.5.4.

If G is a compact Lie group, then

DG=𝕊𝔤≔Σ∞⁢(𝔤+)

where G acts by the adjoint representation.

For example, let 𝕋=U⁡(1)=S1. Then because the adjoint representation of an abelian group is trivial, we have D𝕋=𝕊1 with the trivial action.

Now assume that B⁢G≃(M,m0) for some closed smooth manifold M. For example, if G=ℤ, then B⁢G≃S1. Alternatively, we can consider any closed manifold (M,m0) and let G=Ω⁢M.

Theorem 1.2.5.5 (Atiyah duality).

The dualizing spectrum is given by

DG=𝕊−Tm0⁢M≃𝕊−dimM,

where we extend the construction 𝕊V for any representation of G to a virtual representation. As a functor

B⁢G≃M→𝖲𝗉,

it sends

m↦𝕊−Tm⁢M.
Remark 1.2.5.6.

For any space X (in place of B⁢G), we can define a dualizing spectrum

DX:X→𝖲𝗉.

For example, we can define this functor on connected components because

X≃⨆B⁢Gi.

In particular, we assign DGi to B⁢Gi.

Construction 1.2.5.7.

Let 𝒞 be a stable ∞-category which has all limits and colimits. For any E∈𝖲𝗉 and X∈𝒞, there is an object

E⊗X∈𝒞

defined such that the functor

−⊗X:𝖲𝗉→𝒞

preserves colimits and the composite

𝒮→Σ+∞𝖲𝗉→−⊗X𝒞

is given by the functor

M↦M⊗X=colimMcX.
Definition 1.2.5.8.

Let G∈𝖠𝗅𝗀𝔼1𝗀𝗉⁢(𝒮) and X∈B⁢G. We define the norm map

NmG:(DG⊗𝕊X)h⁢G→Xh⁢G

as the composite
Exercise 1.2.5.9.

Prove that

((Σ+∞⁢G⊗𝕊X)h⁡(1×G))h⁡(G×1)≃Xh⁢G.

This is quite an abstract construction, so we will try to get our hands on it with some examples.

Example 1.2.5.10.

If G is finite and X∈𝒞B⁢G, then the norm map is

(DG⊗X)h⁢G≃Xh⁢G→Xh⁢G.

For example, if 𝒞=𝖲𝗉 and X=H⁢M for an abelian group M with a G-action, then this map is a map

and is induced from the classical norm map

MG→MG[m],↦∑g∈Gg⁢m

from coinvariants to invariants. This follows from the fact that for a general X, the composite

X→Xh⁢G→NmGXh⁢G→X

is the sum over all g∈G of the maps ρg:X→X given by multiplication by g.

Exercise 1.2.5.11.

Prove that if G is finite, the composite

X→Xh⁢G→NmGXh⁢G→X

agrees with the map

∑g∈Gρg:X→X.
Example 1.2.5.12.

When G=𝕋, we get a map

Σ⁢Xh⁢𝕋=(D𝕋⊗X)h⁢𝕋→Xh⁢𝕋.
Theorem 1.2.5.13.

The norm map (DG⊗X)h⁢G→Xh⁢G is an equivalence provided that one of the following conditions holds:

  1. 1.

    B⁢G is a finite CW complex;

  2. 2.

    X is induced, which means that X≃Σ+∞⁢G⊗Y where G acts only on Σ+∞⁢G.

Sketch of proof.

In the first case, all limits in the interchange maps are finite. Because all functors in the composite are exact, we are done.

In the second case, the limits and colimits are still close enough to being finite, so we are done. □

Example 1.2.5.14.

Let B⁢G be a closed manifold M, 𝒞=𝖲𝗉, and X=H⁢ℤ with the trivial action of G. In this case, the norm is a map

(D⁢G⊗X)h⁢G→∼Xh⁢G=H⁢ℤB⁢G.

The target has homotopy groups given by

π∗⁢(H⁢ℤB⁢G)=H−⁣∗⁢(M,ℤ).

The source is explicitly given by

(D⁢G⊗X)h⁢G≅(𝕊−t⁢M⊗H⁢ℤ)h⁢G≃(H⁢ℤ⁢[−n])h⁢G,

where G acts on H⁢Z⁢[−n] non-trivially. This has homotopy groups

π∗⁢((H⁢ℤ⁢[−n])h⁢G)=H∗+n⁢(M,ℤw1)

given by homology with coefficients in the orientation cover. On homotopy groups, this map

H∗+n⁢(M,ℤw1)→∼H−⁣∗⁢(M,ℤ)

is simply Poincaré duality (at least if M is orientable).

If we replace H⁢ℤ by any spectrum, we get Poincaré duality in arbitrary cohomology theories. If X=B⁢G is a finite CW complex, the norm equivalence is a generalized version of Poincaré duality

H∗⁢(X,DX)→H−⁣∗⁢(X).

This can be thought of as being analogous to Serre or Verdier duality in algebraic geometry. If DX is a parameterized sphere (DX=𝕊⁡[n] as underlying spectra), then this is equivalent to X being a Poincaré duality space.

Theorem 1.2.5.15 (Klein).

The natural transformation (called the assembly map)

(DG⊗−)h⁢G→(−)h⁢G

exhibits the functor (DG⊗−)h⁢G as the universal functor over (−)h⁢G which preserves colimits.

Note that this uniquely determines the spectrum DG as an object of 𝖲𝗉B⁢G.

Definition 1.2.5.16.

For an object X∈𝒞B⁢G, we define the Tate object as the cofiber

Xt⁢G≔𝖼𝗈𝖿𝗂𝖻⁡(NmG).
Example 1.2.5.17.

If B⁢G is finite, then Xt⁢G=0 for all X. If G is finite and X=H⁢M for an abelian group M with a G-action, then (H⁢M)t⁢G has homotopy groups given by the Tate cohomology

π∗⁢((H⁢M)t⁢G)=H^−⁣∗⁢(G,M)

of G with coefficients in M.

Exercise 1.2.5.18.

Work out what Tate cohomology is in terms of usual homology and cohomology.

Example 1.2.5.19.

Suppose that 𝒞 is a symmetric monoidal ∞-category such that the tensor product commutes with colimits in both variables separately. Then the functor

(−)t⁢G:𝒞B⁢G→𝒞

admits a (unique) lax symmetric monoidal structure such that the natural transformation

(−)h⁢G→(−)t⁢G

admits a refinement to a symmetric monoidal transformation.

Corollary 1.2.5.20.

If A∈𝖠𝗅𝗀𝔼n⁢(𝒞B⁢G)≃𝖠𝗅𝗀𝔼n⁢(𝒞)B⁢G, then Ah⁢G→At⁢G is a morphism of 𝔼n-algebras.

1.2.6 Tate diagonal

The Tate diagonal is a surprising feature of the world of spectra. Before we discuss it, we will motivate it by discussing abelian groups.

Let A be an abelian group. If we try to write a map of sets

A→A⊗A,x↦x⊗x,

this is not a homomorphism. For example, note that

(x+y)⊗(x+y)=x⊗x+y⊗y+(x⊗y+y⊗x).

Recall now that if Cp is the cyclic group with p elements, there is a norm map

N:(A⊗p)Cp→(A⊗p)Cp,x1⊗⋯⁢xp↦∑σ∈Cpxσ⁡(1)⊗⋯⊗xσ⁡(p).

Note here that the error term of the map x↦x⊗x is in the image of the norm map. Therefore, the “diagonal” x↦x⊗⋯⊗x induces a homormorphism

A→(A⊗p)Cp/N⁡((A⊗p)Cp).

This homomorphism in fact exhibits

(A⊗p)Cp/N⁡((A⊗p)Cp)≅A/p.
Exercise 1.2.6.1.
  1. 1.

    Prove that x↦x⊗p induces a homomorphism

    A→(A⊗p)Cp/N⁡((A⊗p)Cp).
  2. 2.

    Prove that this homomorphism factors through an isomorphism

    A/p→∼(A⊗p)Cp/N⁡((A⊗p)Cp).

We will now discuss the analogous construction for spectra.

Theorem 1.2.6.2.

There is a unique lax symmetric monoidal natural transformation

X→(X⊗p)t⁢Cp.

In the rest of this section, we will attempt to see where this comes from and understand some of its properties.

Lemma 1.2.6.3.

The Singer construction

X↦(X⊗p)t⁢Cp

is an exact functor.

This result is particularly surprising because the p-th tensor power functor is not even additive.

Proof.

First, suppose Y≃X⊕Z. By the binomial theorem, we have

(X⊕Z)⊗p =X⊗p⊕Z⊗p⊕⨁p(X⊗(p−1)⊗Z)⊕⨁(p2)(X⊗(p−2)⊗Z⊗2)⊕⋯

On all of the non-pure terms, the action of Cp on the connected components is free, so these terms are all induced modules over Cp. These terms vanish after taking Tate fixed points.

In general, consider a cofiber sequence X→Y→Z as a “two-stage filtration” on Y of the form

where Z appears as the associated graded term. We then obtain a filtration on Y⊗p of the form

X⊗p→⨁X⊗(p−1)⊗Y→⋯→⨁X⊗Y⊗(p−1)→Y⊗p.

There is a monoidal structure on filtered objects called the Day convolution structure which produces this diagram from our filtered object. The associated graded terms are given by

X⊗p,…,⨁pX⊗Z⊗(p−1),Z⊗p.

Applying Tate fixed points, the associated graded terms are now of the form

(X⊗p)t⁢Cp,0,…,0,(Z⊗p)t⁢Cp.

This implies that we have a cofiber sequence

(X⊗p)t⁢Cp→(Y⊗p)t⁢Cp→(Z⊗p)t⁢Cp.□
Remark 1.2.6.4.

The Singer construction commutes with suspension as

((Σ⁢X)⊗p)t⁢Cp≃Σ⁢(X⊗p)t⁢Cp.

We can write

(Σ⁢X)⊗p≃𝕊p⊗X⊗p,

but the action of Cp involves a nontrivial action on 𝕊p, where we take the suspension spectrum of the one-point compactification of the regular representation of Cp. In fact, we have (𝕊p)t⁢Cp≃(𝕊1)t⁢Cp, where S1 has the trivial action.

Lemma 1.2.6.5 (Stable Yoneda Lemma).

Let 𝒞 be a stable ∞-category. We consider the stable ∞-category 𝖥𝗎𝗇𝖾𝗑⁢(𝒞,𝖲𝗉) of exact functors to 𝖲𝗉. Taking mapping spectra, there exists a natural equivalence

𝗆𝖺𝗉𝖥𝗎𝗇𝖾𝗑⁢(𝒞,𝖲𝗉)⁢(𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(X,−),F)≃F⁡(X).
Proof sketch.

We will reduce this to the 1-categorical Yoneda lemma. A natural transformation 𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(X,−)→F is simply a sequence of natural transformations on the n-th underlying spaces with some compatibility conditions. More precisely, we have natural transformations

𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(Σ−n⁢X,−)→Ω∞⁢Σn⁢F⁢(−),

which by the ordinary Yoneda lemma yields a sequence of points in

Ω∞⁢Σn⁢F⁢(Σ−n⁢X)≃Ω∞⁢F⁢(X).

In other words, we have an equivalence of spaces

𝖬𝖺𝗉𝖥𝗎𝗇𝖾𝗑⁢(𝒞,𝖲𝗉)⁢(𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(X,−),F)≃Ω∞⁢F⁢(X).□

Natural transformations X→(X⊗p)t⁢Cp correspond to maps 𝕊→(𝕊⊗p)t⁢Cp≃𝕊t⁢Cp. There is a natural choice of map like this given by

𝕊≃𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(Σ+∞⁢pt,𝕊)→𝕊h⁢Cp≃𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(Σ+∞⁢Cp,𝕊)→𝕊t⁢Cp.

Note that there are other maps 𝕊→𝕊t⁢Cp, for example the zero map. However, we need a map which preserves the lax symmetric monoidal structure, and the unique such map is the one we have just given.

Lemma 1.2.6.6.

The functor 𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(𝕊,−) is initial among all lax symmetric monoidal exact functors 𝖲𝗉→𝖲𝗉.

We are now ready to discuss some properties of the Tate diagonal. In particular, we will not prove anything.

Theorem 1.2.6.7.

For a bounded below X, the morphism

X→(X⊗p)t⁢Cp

exhibits (X⊗p)t⁢Cp as Xp∧. In particular, (X⊗p)t⁢Cp is bounded below.

In particular, we see that 𝕊t⁢Cp≃𝕊p∧. This is completely different from Tate cohomology for abelian groups and is a special form of the Segal conjecture. Proofs of these results rely on the Adams spectral sequence because the Tate spectral sequences is too messy.

The Tate construction also allows us to define a version of Frobenius on 𝔼∞-ring spectra.

Definition 1.2.6.8.

For an 𝔼∞-ring spectrum R, we have the Tate-valued Frobenius

R→Δ(R⊗p)t⁢Cp→μt⁢CpRt⁢Cp

using the fact that multiplication R⊗p→R is equivariant. This follows from the fact that a morphism (R⊗p)h⁢Cp→R is encoded in the definition of an 𝔼∞-algebra.

We should think about this as an analogue of the morphism

R→R/p,x↦xp

for an ordinary commutative ring R.

Exercise 1.2.6.9.

Prove that it is necessary that R is commutative and that the target is reduced by p. Also prove that x↦xp is a ring homomorphism R→R/p.

Applying the Tate-valued Frobenius to

𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(Σ+∞⁢X,E)

for some space X and 𝔼∞-algebra E, we obtain power operations. For example, Steenrod operations and Adams operations arise in this way.

2 (Topological) cyclic homology

2.1 Classical Hochschild and cyclic homology

In this section, we discuss Hochschild homology, (negative, periodic) cyclic homology, the HKR theorem, and related topics.

2.1.1 Hochschild homology

Let k be a field and R be a k- algebra.

Definition 2.1.1.1.

The Hochschild homology of R is the homology of the complex

𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)≔(⋯→∂R⊗kR→∂R),

where the differential is given by

∂(a0⊗⋯⊗an)≔ a0⁢a1⊗⋯⊗an
−a0⊗a1⁢a2⊗⋯⊗an
⋯
+(−1)n⁢an⁢a0⊗⋯⊗an−1.
Remark 2.1.1.2.

This seems related to what happens when you multiply elements placed on an S1 as in Figure 2.1. In fact, we will see later that there is a connection to the actual S1.

Example 2.1.1.3.

For now, set R=k. In this case, we have

𝖧𝖧⁡(k/k) =(⋯→k→k),

where the differentials are alternating sums of 1 and −1. In fact, we see that the complex is

𝖧𝖧⁡(k/k)=(⋯→0k→idk→0k),

and therefore the Hochschild homology is

𝖧𝖧∗⁢(k/k)={k∗=00otherwise.
Example 2.1.1.4.

Because the last differential is given by a⊗b↦a⁢b−b⁢a, we see that

𝖧𝖧0⁢(R/k)=R/[R,R].

In particular, if R is commutative, we have

𝖧𝖧0⁢(R/k)=R.

In this case, we have

𝖧𝖧1⁢(R/k)=R⊗kRIm∂≅ΩR/k1.

We will now recall the definition of the module of Kähler differentials.

Definition 2.1.1.5.

The module of Kähler differentials of a commutative ring R is the module ΩR/k1 generated by dx for all x∈R subject to the following relations:

  1. 1.

    For all x,y∈R, we have d⁡(x+y)=dx+dy;

  2. 2.

    For all x,y∈R, we have d⁡(x⁢y)=x⁢dy+y⁢dx;

  3. 3.

    For all x∈k, we have dx=0.

Therefore, we see that ΩR/k1 receives a universal k-linear derivation from R.

There is at most one map

𝖧𝖧1⁢(R/k)→ΩR/k1x⊗y↦x⋅dy.
Exercise 2.1.1.6.

Check that this is an isomorphism.

We will now prove some more properties of Hochschild homology.

Lemma 2.1.1.7.

If R is commutative, then 𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R) has the structure of a strictly graded-commutative ring. Here, this means that x2=0 for any x of odd degree, which is only relevant in characterisic 2.

Proof.

The Hochschild complex 𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k) in fact comes from a simplicial commutative ring

where the face maps are the components of the differential ∂. The desired result then follows by Theorem A.1.0.2. □

On the de Rham side, there is also a multiplicative structure.

Definition 2.1.1.8.

The de Rham complex is the exterior algebra

ΩR/k∗ ≔ΛR∗⁢ΩR/k1
=⨁k≥0ΛRk⁢ΩR/k1
=SymR⁡ΩR/k1⁢[1]x2=0,x∈ΩR/k1.

By extending from degree 1, we obtain a map ΩR/k∗→𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k).

Theorem 2.1.1.9 (Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg).

If R/k has cotangent complex concentrated in degree 0, then the map

ΩR/k∗→𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k)

is an isomorphism.

We will discuss the cotangnet complex later, but for now we may think that R is a smooth or ind-smooth k-algebra.

Remark 2.1.1.10.

The differential on ΩR/k∗ does not play a role here. Studying what it corresponds to on the Hochschild side will leade us to cyclic homology.

Exercise 2.1.1.11.

Find an explicit description of Ωk⁡[x1,…,xn]/k∗ and in particular show that it is concentrated in degrees at most n.

We will now extend to the case when k is an arbitrary commutative ring. This will lead to flatness issues, so we will fix this by taking derived tensor products. For now, we will let R be a dg-algebra over k which is K-flat. This is a flatness condition, but when R is bounded below, it agrees with levelwise flatness. Over ℤ, it always agrees with levelwise flatness. For such an R, we define the Hochschild complex by

𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)≔Tot⁡(⋯→R⊗kR→R).

If R is not K-flat, we will simply replace it by a K-flat resolution R♭ and define

𝖧𝖧(R/k)≔𝖧𝖧(R♭.k).

This is well-defined up to quasi-isomorphism.

Proposition 2.1.1.12.

For a dg-algebra R, there is a quasi-isomorphism

𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)≃R⊗R⊗k𝕃Rop𝕃R.
Remark 2.1.1.13.

This is usually called Shukla homology, but we will not make this distinction here.

Proof.

Replacing R by a flat resolution, we consider the complex

Tot⁡(⋯→R⊗kR⊗kR→R⊗kR)≃R.

The differentials are given by multiplying adjacent terms, but without the an⁢a0 term (think configurations on an interval). This complex is usually called the bar complex. Applying −⊗R⊗kRopR, the resulting total complex computes the desired complex R⊗R⊗kRop𝕃R, but it also computes 𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k). □

Lemma 2.1.1.14.

If R is a dg-algebra which arises from a simplicial commutative k-algebra, then 𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k) also comes from a simplicial commutative k-algebra. In particular, the Hochschild homology groups 𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k) form a strictly graded-commutative k-algebra.

Proof.

We replace R by a flat simplicial commutative k-algebra. Then 𝖧𝖧⁡(Rn/k) gives a bisimplicial commutative k-algebra. The total complex is then quasi-isomorphic to the diagonal, which is clearly simplicial. □

Lemma 2.1.1.15.

If A,B are dg-algebras, then

𝖧𝖧⁡(A⊗𝕃B/k)≃𝖧𝖧⁡(A/k)⊗k𝕃𝖧𝖧⁡(B/k).
Remark 2.1.1.16.

If R is commutative, then setting A=B=R gives a multiplication map on 𝖧𝖧 via the multiplication of R.

Proof.

Because 𝖧𝖧⁡(A/k) and 𝖧𝖧⁡(B/k) are simplicial dg-algebras, the tensor product

𝖧𝖧⁡(A/k)⊗k𝕃𝖧𝖧⁡(B/k)

is a bisimplicial dg-algebra. Taking the total complex in all three directions, the result is quasi-isomorphic to the diagonal, which is precisely

𝖧𝖧⁡(A⊗k𝕃B).□

We are now ready to prove the HKR theorem for polynomial rings. As we will see later, we will reduce the general case to this one.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.1.9 for polynomial rings.

In the case of R=k⁡[x], we have

Ωk⁡[x]/k∗=k⁡[x]⊗Λ⁡(dx).

Then we only need to check that 𝖧𝖧⁡(k⁡[x]/k) vanishes in degree greater than 1. This is given by

𝖧𝖧⁡(k⁡[x]/k) =k⁡[x]⊗k⁡[x]⊗kk⁡[x]𝕃k⁡[x]
=k⁡[x]⊗k⁡[a,b]𝕃k⁡[x].

We have the resolution

k⁡[a,b]→⋅(a−b)k⁡[a,b]

of k⁡[x], and this gives the desired result.

For R=k⁡[x1,…,xn] This is simply a tensor product

R=k⁡[x1]⊗k⋯⊗kk⁡[xn],

so because both sides of the HKR theorem commute with tensor products, we obtain the desired result.

Finally, if R=k⁡[xi|i∈I], we write R as a filtered colimit of finitely-generated polynomial algebras by writing the set {xi|i∈I} of generators as a filtered colimit of its finite subsets. Because both sides commute with filtered colimits, we are done. □

We will now turn to an extremely non-smooth example.

Proposition 2.1.1.17.

We have

𝖧𝖧∗⁢(𝔽p/ℤ)=𝔽p⁢⟨x⟩,

where the ⟨x⟩ means the free divided power algebra generated by x.

Proof.

We will compute the derived tensor product

𝔽p⊗𝔽p⊗𝕃𝔽p𝔽p.

We will resolve 𝔽p by the dg-algebra

ℤ⁡[ε]/ε2,∂ε=p,|ε|=1.

The tensor product is then given by

A≃𝔽p⊗𝕃𝔽p≃𝔽p⁢[ε]/ε2.

We will resolve 𝔽p as an A-algebra by

A⁡⟨x⟩=A⁡[x1,x2,…]xi⁢xj=(i+ji)⁢xi+j,∂xi=ε⁢xi−1,|xi|=2⁢i,

and the desired result follows by taking the tensor product. □

2.1.2 The Connes operator

We will describe an operator on 𝖧𝖧 which corresponds to the de Rham differential. Recall that the de Rham differential

d:ΩR/k∗→ΩR/k∗+1

is induced from the universial derivation d:R→ΩR/k1 by the Leibniz rule.

Definition 2.1.2.1.

Let R be an associative k-algebra. We define a k-linear map

B:𝖧𝖧⁢(R/k)n→𝖧𝖧⁢(R/k)n+1

by the formula

r0⊗⋯⊗rn↦∑σ∈Cn+1(−1)n⁢σ⁢(0)⁢(1⊗rσ+(−1)n⁢rσ⊗1),

where we define

rσ≔rσ⁡(0)⊗⋯⊗rσ⁡(n).

This formula is related to the cyclic objects introduced by Connes, and there is a way to think about it systematically in the topological setting, which we will discuss later.

Exercise 2.1.2.2.

Check that

  1. 1.

    B2=0;

  2. 2.

    dB+B⁢d=0.

The operator B equips 𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k) with the structure of a dg-module over the dg-algebra

A≔k⁡[b]/b2,|b|=1,∂=0.

Note that if 𝕋=U⁡(1) is the circle group, then we have

A=H∗⁢(𝕋,k).

We then see that 𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k) is a graded module over k⁡[b]/b2, and in particular that there is an operator

B:𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k)→𝖧𝖧∗+1⁢(R/k)

satisfying B2=0.

Warning 2.1.2.3.

One might object that we only defined the Connes operator only for algebras concentrated in degree 0, but with some careful thought we can define B for dg-algebras R/k.

We need the following fact.

Lemma 2.1.2.4.

If R is commutative, then B is a derivation. In particular, it satisfies the graded Leibniz rule

B⁡(x⁢y)=B⁡(x)⁢y+(−1)|x|⁢x⁢B⁢(y).
Warning 2.1.2.5.

The Connes operator is not true on the complex 𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k). It is true up to coherent homotopy, but proving this is very hard. Instead, we will later use the topological enhancement to understand this.

Proposition 2.1.2.6.

The map

ΩR/k∗→𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k)

sends the de Rham differential d to the Connes operator B. In other words, the diagram

commutes.

Proof.

The map ΩR/k∗→𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k) is determined by its effect in degrees 0 and 1. In degree 0, it is given by the identity

R→𝖧𝖧0⁢(R/k)=R,

and in degree 1, it is given by

ΩR/k1→𝖧𝖧1⁢(R/k)=R⊗kR∼x⁢dy↦[x⊗y].

Therefore, it is enough to check that the diagram

commutes. Note that for any r∈R, we see that all signs in the definition of B are +1, so we have

B⁡(r)=[1⊗r]+[r⊗1].

This corresponds to the element

1⋅dr+r⋅d⁢1=dr∈ΩR/k1.

We conclude by using the fact that the de Rham differential is uniquely determined by being a derivation and its effect on R. □

Remark 2.1.2.7.

Sometimes in the rest of these notes, we will denote the Connes operator by d. If this causes confusion, we will call it B.

Example 2.1.2.8.

For 𝖧𝖧∗⁢(𝔽p/ℤ)=𝔽p⁢⟨x⟩ with x in degree 2, the Connes operator acts trivially for degree reasons.

Question 2.1.2.9.

Does this mean that it acts trivially (maybe up to homotopy or quasi-isomorphism) on 𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p,ℤ)?

The answer to this question is in fact no, and we will see this by taking a (derived) reduction mod p. This means that we will consider

𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)⫽p≔𝖧𝖧⁡(Fp)⊗ℤ𝕃𝔽p.

Letting A act trivially on 𝔽p, we obtain a structure of an A-module on 𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)⫽p. We compute

𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)⫽p ≃𝖧𝖧⁡(Fp)⊗ℤ(Λℤ⁢(ε),|ε|=1,∂ε=p)
≃𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)⊗𝔽pΛ𝔽p⁢(ε).

This implies that

H∗⁢(𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)⫽p) ≃𝖧𝖧∗⁢(𝔽p)⊗𝔽pΛ𝔽p⁢(ε)
≃𝔽p⁢⟨x⟩⊗𝔽pΛ𝔽p⁢(ε).
Proposition 2.1.2.10.

Writing the divided power γn⁢(x) as x[n], we have B⁡(x[n])=0 and B⁡(ε)=x.

Note that this implies that

B⁡(ε⁢x[n])=x⁢x[n]=(n+1)⁢x[n+1].
Proof.

The map 𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)→𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)⫽p is compatible with B, and therefore we obtain B⁡(x[n])=0 in homology.

Now recall that we computed

𝖧𝖧∗⁢(𝔽p)=𝔽p⁢⟨x⟩

by replacing 𝔽p by (Λℤ⁢(ε),∂ε=p), so we write the complex

⋯→∂Λℤ⁢(ε)⊗Λℤ⁢(ε)→∂Λℤ⁢(ε).

Writing out the full double complex, we obtain

The class x is given by 1⊗ε−ε⊗1. Applying B, we obtain

B⁡(ε)=1⊗ε−ε⊗1.

After reducing mod p, we can replace all copies of ℤ by 𝔽p and ε becomes a cycle, and we obtain B⁡(ε)=x. □

2.1.3 Periodic and cyclic homology

In the anology between Hochschild homology and the de Rham complex, we will now discuss cyclic homology, which will be analogous to algebraic de Rham cohomology.

We will work with derived functors in the category 𝖣𝖦𝖬𝗈𝖽A. The homotopy theory we will work with is inverting quasi-isomorphisms, which means we will consider the ∞-category

𝖬𝗈𝖽A⁢(𝒟⁡(k)).
Definition 2.1.3.1.

Let R be a k-algebra.

  1. 1.

    The cyclic homology of R is

    𝖧𝖢∗⁢(R/k)≔H∗⁢(k⊗A𝕃𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k))=Tor∗A⁡(k,𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)).

    This will not play any role in these notes.

  2. 2.

    The negative cyclic homology of R is

    𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(R/k)≔RHomA⁡(k,𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k))=ExtA−⁣∗⁡(k,𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)).

    This is more important than cyclic homology, and topological cyclic homology will be an analog of this rather than of cyclic homology. Also, note that 𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(R/k) is a module over ExtA∗⁡(k,k)=k⁡[t], where |t|=−2.

  3. 3.

    The periodic cyclic homology (or periodic homology) of R is

    𝖧𝖯∗⁢(R/k)=𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(R/k)⁢[t−1].
Exercise 2.1.3.2.

Show that ExtA∗⁡(k,k)≅k⁡[t], where |t|=−2.

Note that the definition we gave is not the standard one in the literature, which involves double complexes. We may wonder if these definitions are equivalent.

Proposition 2.1.3.3.

For any k-algebra R, we have

𝖧𝖢−⁢(R/k)≃(𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)⁢⟦t⟧,∂+t⁢B),

where ∂+t⁢B is defined as

x⁢ti↦(∂x)⁢ti+(B⁢x)⁢ti+1

for x∈𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k) (this is basically saying that ∂(t)=0). Moreover, we have

𝖧𝖯⁡(R/k)≃(𝖧𝖧⁡(R)⁢⦇t⦈,∂+t⁢B).
Proof.

We will resolve k as an A-algebra by

C=A⁡{x0,x1,…},|xk|=2⁢k,

where we declare that

∂(xk)=b⁢xk−1.

Note that C also has the structure of a coalgebra with coproduct given by

Δ⁡(xk)=∑i+j=k∑i+j=kxi⊗xj.

This implies that

RHomA⁡(k,𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)) =Hom¯A⁢(C,𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k))
=(𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)⁢⟦t⟧,∂+t⁢B).

Here, we use the fact that ti is the dual of the element xi, and therefore because the differential on C is just b and lowers the x-degree by 1, dually it will be B and raise the t-degree by 1. The formula for 𝖧𝖯⁡(R/k) follows by inverting t. □

Remark 2.1.3.4.

This argument works more generally to obtain RHom⁡(k,H) for an arbitrary H∈𝖣𝖦𝖬𝗈𝖽A.

Remark 2.1.3.5.

A is a Hopf algebra with couint

ε:A→kε⁡(b)=0

and coproduct Δ:A→A⊗A given by

Δ⁡(b)=1⊗b+b⊗1.

This implies that RHom¯A⁢(k,−) is a lax symmetric monoidal functor (here, note that k is the unit in the category of dg A-modules) and as such is given by

H↦(H⁡⟦t⟧,∂+t⁢B)

as a lax symmetric monoidal functor. Moreover, if C is an algebra object in 𝖣𝖦𝖬𝗈𝖽A, i.e. C is a dg algebra and B satisfies the Leibniz rule, then RHom¯A⁢(k,C) is a dg algebra.

Warning 2.1.3.6.

Even if R is commutative, B is not a derivation on 𝖧𝖧⁡(R), so we cannot simply argue that negative cyclic and periodic homology have products. This is true up to chain homotopy, however, but this is still not enough to obtain a product. We will see that B is a derivation up to coherent homotopy, but we run into issues with the formality of A, which will require working with S1 to resolve.

Instead of doing all of that, we will use the hack that (𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)⁢⟦t⟧,∂+t⁢B) has a product up to chain homotopy. This implies that 𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(R/k) and 𝖧𝖯∗⁢(R/k) are graded commutative algebras.

Our goal now is to enhance the HKR theorem (Theorem 2.1.1.9). For this, we will need de Rham cohomology.

Definition 2.1.3.7.

Let R be a commutative k-algebra. The de Rham cohomology of R relative to k is defined as

H𝖽𝖱∗⁢(R/k)≔H∗⁢(Ω∗⁢(R/k),d).
Remark 2.1.3.8.

Since we are working with commutative rings (equivalently, affine schemes), every term in the de Rham complex is acyclic by vanishing of higher cohomology on affines, so we are just taking global sections. However, this invariant is more interesting for schemes X/k by upgrading the de Rham complex to a complex of sheaves.

Theorem 2.1.3.9.

Assume that ℚ⊆k and that LR/k is flat and concentrated in degree 0. Then there are natural isomorphisms

𝖧𝖯∗⁢(R/k)≅H𝖽𝖱∗⁢(R/k)⁢⦇t⦈,

where |t|=−2 and

𝖧𝖢n−⁢(R/k)≅Z𝖽𝖱n⁢(R/k)⊕∏i≥1H𝖽𝖱n+2⁢i⁢(R/k).
Exercise 2.1.3.10.

Describe the map 𝖧𝖢∗−→𝖧𝖯∗ in this case and check that it exhibits

𝖧𝖯∗≅𝖧𝖢∗−⁢[t−1].
Remark 2.1.3.11.

Because this is again relatively boring for rings, the interesting statement is that for a scheme X/k with LX.k being flat and concentrated in degree 0, we have

𝖧𝖯∗⁢(X/k)≅H𝖽𝖱∗⁢(X,k)⁢⦇t⦈.
Remark 2.1.3.12.

We can drop the flatness assumption on R if we replace de Rham cohomology with a Hodge-completed derived de Rham cohomology following Bhatt-Morrow-Scholze, but this is of course extremely complicated.

Remark 2.1.3.13.

The statement of Theorem 2.1.3.9 is false if k is not characteric 0.

Proof.

We will give a classical proof. It is possible to give a fancier proof using nonabelian derived functors.

Consider a chain-level map

μ:𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)→ΩR/k∗

given by

r0⊗r1⊗⋯⊗rn↦1n!⁢r0⁢dr1⁢⋯⁢drn.
Lemma 2.1.3.14.

This μ is an A-linear map of commutative dg algebras

(𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k),∂,B)→(ΩR/k∗,0,d).
Proof of Lemma.

We compute

μ⁡(∂(r0⊗⋯⊗rn))
= μ(r0r1⊗r2⊗⊗rn−r0⊗r1r2⊗⋯⊗rn+⋯±rnr0⊗r1⊗⋯⊗rn−1)
= r0⁢r1⁢dr2⁢⋯⁢drn
−r0⁢d⁢(r1⁢r2)⁢dr3⁢⋯⁢drn
+⋯
= r0⁢r1⁢dr2⁢⋯⁢drn
−r0⁢r1⁢dr2⁢⋯⁢drn
+⋯
=0.

Compatibility with B and d is given by the equation

μ⁡(B⁡(r0⊗⋯⊗rn)) =∑σ∈Cn+1(−1)n⁢σ⁢(0)⁢μ⁢(1⊗rσ±rσ⊗1)
=1(n+1)!⁢∑σ∈Cn+1sign⁡(σ)⁢drσ⁡(0)⁢⋯⁢drσ⁡(n)
=1n!⁢dr0⊗⋯⊗drn
=d⁡(1n!⁢r0⁢dr1⁢⋯⁢drn)
=d⁡(μ⁡(r0⊗⋯⊗rn)).

We conclude with the following exercise.

Exercise 2.1.3.15.

Check that μ is multiplicative with respect to the shuffle product on the left and the wedge product of forms on the right. □

Using the lemma, we see that

ΩR/k∗→𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k)→H∗⁢(μ)ΩR/k∗

is the identity, so the statement follows from Theorem 2.1.1.9. □

We are now ready to prove Theorem 2.1.3.9.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.3.9.

We simply compute

𝖧𝖯∗⁢(R/k) =H∗⁢(𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)⁢⦇t⦈,∂+t⁢B)
≃H∗⁢(ΩR/k∗⁢⦇t⦈,t⁢d)
≅H𝖽𝖱∗⁢(R/k)⁢⦇t⦈.

Applying the same strategy to negative cyclic homology, we obtain

𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(R/k)≅H∗⁢(ΩR/k∗⁢⟦t⟧,t⁢d).□

We still want to deal with arbitary k (so not in characteristic 0).

Construction 2.1.3.16.

We have the Postnikov filtration

τ≥⁣∙⁢𝖧𝖧⁢(R/k)

of 𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k) as an A-module, which is compatible with B and leads to a filtration of

(τ≥⁣∙⁢𝖧𝖧⁢(R/k)⁢⦇t⦈,∂+t⁢B).

𝖧𝖯⁡(R/k).

This leads to a multiplicative, conditionally convergent spectral sequence

E2=𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k)⁢⦇t⦈⟹𝖧𝖯∗⁢(R/k).

The E3-page is given by

H∗⁢(𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/k),B)⁢⦇t⦈⟹𝖧𝖯∗⁢(R/k).

If R has flat cotangent complex, then this is

E3=H𝖽𝖱∗⁢(R/k)⁢⦇t⦈⟹𝖧𝖯∗⁢(R/k).

We will now return to the example of 𝔽p over ℤ. First, we need to upgrade divided powers to divided power series.

Definition 2.1.3.17.

Let R be a commutative ring. We define the divided power series algebra R⁢⟨⟨x⟩⟩ as the completion of R⁢⟨x⟩ at the filtration generated by the divided powers of x (note this is not an adic completion).

Proposition 2.1.3.18.

For R=𝔽p, we have

𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ)≅ℤp⁢[t]⁢⟨⟨x⟩⟩/(x⁢t−p),|x|=2,|t|=−2.

In addition, we have

𝖧𝖯∗⁢(𝔽p/ℤ) ≅ℤp⁢[t±]⁢⟨⟨x⟩⟩/(x⁢t−p)
≅(ℤp⁢⟨⟨y⟩⟩/(y−p))⁢[t±],

where y has degree 0.

Remark 2.1.3.19.

Note that we have

𝖧𝖯0⁢(𝔽p/ℤ)≅𝖧𝖢0−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ)≅ℤp⁢⟨⟨y⟩⟩/(y−p),

which is obtained by adjoining divided powers of p to ℤp. Because ℤp already has divided powers of p, the element y[p]−ppp! is p-torsion. In fact, we have

ℤp⁢⟨y⟩/(y−p)≅ℤp⁢⟨z⟩/z,

where we should think of z as y−p.

What we have seen is that the negative cyclic and periodic cyclic homology of 𝔽p is very unpleasant. The situation will improve when we consider the topological version of everything. Also, in fact, 𝖧𝖯∗⁢(𝔽p/ℤ) is the 2-periodic derived de Rham cohomology of 𝔽p.

Proof.

Recall that 𝖧𝖧∗⁢(𝔽p/ℤ)≅𝔽p⁢⟨x⟩. We also recall the spectral sequence coming from the Postnikov filtration, which reads

𝔽p⁢⟨x⟩⁢[t]⟹𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ).

The E2-page of the spectral sequence is given below, where the horizontal direction is powers of t and the vertical direction is divided powers of x. We also use dots to denote copies of 𝔽p.

Because everything is in even degree, the spectral sequence collapses at the E2-page. Therefore, 𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ) has a filtration with associated graded given by 𝔽p⁢⟨x⟩⁢[t].

There is an additive extension problem and a multiplicative extension problem. We will obtain a copy of ℤp by using the diagonal (with slope 1) entries, and we also need to check that divided powers lift from the associated graded.

The connective cover of 𝖧𝖢−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ) can be represented by a simplicial commutative ring. Later, we will study everything using homotopy theory and see that the Connes operator comes from an S1-action on animated rings, so we can just take homotopy fixed points to obtain 𝖧𝖢−. In any case, the connective cover admits divided powers on positive degree homotopy groups. In particular, every choice of x,t∈𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ) yields a map

ℤ⁡⟨x⟩⁢[t]→𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ).

If we can find x,t such that 𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ), then this map induces an isomorphism on associated gradeds of the map

ℤ⁡⟨x⟩/(x⁢t−p)→𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ).

Because the filtration on 𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ) is complete, completing ℤ⁢⟨x⟩/(x⁢t−p) yields the desired result.

Now we will recall the computation of 𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p/ℤ). We first resolved 𝔽p by

𝔽p≃(Λℤ⁢(ε),∂ε=p).

In 𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p/ℤ), we have x=B⁢ε, ∂x=0, and B⁢x=0. It follows that in 𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p/ℤ), we have a cycle x representing x∈H⁢H∗⁢(𝔽p/ℤ). Using the fact that

𝖧𝖢−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ)=(𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p/ℤ)⁢⟦t⟧,∂+t⁢B),

we calculate

(∂+t⁢B)⁢ε⁢p+t⁢x,

and therefore p=t⁢x in 𝖧𝖢∗−⁢(𝔽p/ℤ). □

Remark 2.1.3.20.

One can also deduce this entire computation using the fact that

(𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p/ℤ),∂,B)≃(ℤ⁡[ε]ε2⁢⟨x⟩,∂ε=p∂x=0,B⁢ε=xB⁢x=0).
Remark 2.1.3.21.

We have not talked at all about cyclic homology, but there is a long exact sequence

which computes 𝖧𝖢⁡(R/k). This comes from a cofiber sequence, or distinguished triangle.

2.1.4 The HKR theorem

We will now discuss the cotangent complex using nonabelian derived functors and prove the HKR theorem.

Let 𝒞 be a 1-category, which is generated by compact projective objects. Here, an object K in compact projective if

Hom⁡(K,−)

preserves filtered colimits and reflexive coequalizers, which are diagrams of the form

Note that this notion doesn’t really make sense for ∞-categories. Being generated by compact projective objects means that all

Hom⁡(K,−)

detect isomorphisms.

We can now pass from 𝒞 to the full subcategory on compact projective objects. If 𝒞=𝖲𝖾𝗍, then we get finite sets, and if 𝖢=𝖬𝗈𝖽R, then we get finitely generated projective modules. We can then construct the animation of 𝒞, which is given by

𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝒞)=𝖥𝗎𝗇Π⁢((𝒞𝖼𝗉)op,𝒮),

where 𝒮 denotes the ∞-category of anima (spaces or simplicial sets). Some properties of this include the following:

  • •

    The category 𝒞𝖼𝗉 of compact projective objects is a full subcategory of 𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝒞), and so is the ind-category 𝖨𝗇𝖽⁡(𝒞𝖼𝗉).

  • •

    A general object of 𝒞 can be represented as the geometric realization of a simplicial diagram with entries in 𝖨𝗇𝖽⁡(𝒞𝖼𝗉).

  • •

    If X is compact projective object of 𝒞 and Yj are any ind-compact projective objects, then the mapping space

    𝖬𝖺𝗉𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝒞)⁢(X,colimj∈ΔopYj)=colimj∈Δop𝖬𝖺𝗉𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝒞)⁢(X,Yj)

    is a simplicial set, so taking the geometric realization gives us a space.

Example 2.1.4.1.

If 𝒞=𝖲𝖾𝗍, functors are determined by their effect on the singleton set, so we just get 𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝖲𝖾𝗍)=𝖲𝗉𝖺𝖼𝖾𝗌.

Example 2.1.4.2.

The non-negative derived category 𝒟⁢(𝒜)≥0 of an abelian category with enough compact projectives is equivalent to the animation 𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝒜). One advantage of this description is that any functor out of 𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝒜) preserving filtered colimits and reflexive coequalizers is simply a functor out of the 1-category 𝒞𝖼𝗉. For example, if we have a nonadditive functor

F:𝒜→ℬ(↪𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(ℬ)),

this will extend to a functor preserving filtered colimits and geometric realizations denoted by

L⁢F:𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝒜)→𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(ℬ).
Example 2.1.4.3.

For any commutative ring R, there is a functor

ΛRn:𝖬𝗈𝖽R→𝖬𝗈𝖽R

taking a module to its n-th exterior power. This is clearly nonadditive, but there is a derived functor

L⁢ΛRn:𝒟⁢(R)≥0→𝒟⁢(R)≥0.

We cannot compute by resolving chain complexes, so instead we will represent an object by a simplicial diagram of projective modules and then applying ΛRn levelwise.

For example, consider R=ℤ. We will attempt to resolve ℤ/n, and this is resolved by the chain complex

ℤ→𝑛ℤ.

Applying the Dold-Kan correspondence, we obtain a simplicial object
Exercise 2.1.4.4.
  1. 1.

    Find a levelwise projective simplicial abelian group whose complex is quasi-isomorphic to ℤ/n⁡[0].

  2. 2.

    Compute L⁢Λℤ2⁢(ℤ/n). Hint: compute Hi for i≤2 by hand and then find a different reason for the vanishing for higher i.

If we apply Λℤ2 to this, we obtain a simplicial diagram

which is simply given by

which is equivalent to ℤ/n⁡[1]. Note that this is not equivalent to applying Λℤ2 levelwise to the chain complex we started with, and that a functor commutes with Dold-Kan only if it is additive.

One advantage of this animation language is that we can discuss animation for categories which have no linear structure. For example, we have

𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀) =𝖥𝗎𝗇Π⁢((𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖼𝗉)op,𝒮)
≅𝖥𝗎𝗇Π⁢((𝖯𝗈𝗅𝗒𝖿𝗀)op,𝒮).

Clearly we see that the ind-compact projective objects

𝖨𝗇𝖽⁡(𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖼𝗉)=𝖯𝗈𝗅𝗒

are simply all polynomial rings. Therefore, we will represent objects by simplicial diagrams of polynomial rings. For example, we have

𝖬𝖺𝗉𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀)⁢(ℤ⁡[x],colimΔopYi)=colimΔopYi

extracts the underlying simplicial set (in fact a simplicial abelian group). This give some version of non-negative complexes with ring structure.

Warning 2.1.4.5.

This does not agree with commutative ring objects in 𝒟⁡(ℤ).

The universal property is that

𝖥𝗎𝗇geom,filtered⁢(𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀),𝒟) =𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(𝖯𝗈𝗅𝗒𝖿𝗀,𝒟)
=𝖥𝗎𝗇filtered⁢(𝖯𝗈𝗅𝗒,𝒟).

This allows us to define nonabelian derived functors by defining functors on polynomial rings which preserve filtered colimits.

Example 2.1.4.6.

The functor 𝖧𝖧(−/ℤ):𝖯𝗈𝗅𝗒→𝒟(ℤ)≥0 commutes with filtered colimits. Therefore, it extends to a functor

L⁢𝖧𝖧:𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀)→𝒟⁢(ℤ)≥0.

If we apply it to an ordinary commutative ring, this agrees with our previous definiion of Hochschild homology. In fact, it agrees for all animated rings by considering the associated dg-algebra.

Remark 2.1.4.7.

There is a way to define Hochschild homology in ∞-categories in much greater generality which does not require animated rings.

Question 2.1.4.8.

Is there a way to extend the HKR theorem to general rings using non-abelian derived functors?

Construction 2.1.4.9.

For any C∈𝒟⁡(ℤ), we can cut off homology groups using the functor τ≥n:𝒟⁡(ℤ)→𝒟⁡(ℤ). This produces a map

τ≥n⁢C→C

which has the following properties:

  • •

    The map is an isomorphism on Hi for i≥n;

  • •

    For all i<n, we have Hi⁢(τ≥n⁢C)=0.

One explicit construction of this is to replace everything in degree <n by 0 and to replace the degree n part with the cycles.

Exercise 2.1.4.10.

Construct the functor τ≥n:𝒟⁡(ℤ)→𝒟⁡(ℤ) using an adjunction.

We in fact have a map τ≥n+1⁢C→τ≥n⁢C, and the cofiber is given by

Cofiber⁡(τ≥n+1⁢C→τ≥n⁢C)≃Hn⁢(C)⁢[n].

For polynomial rings R, we have a diagram

Therefore, we can try to compute Hochschild homology using the machinery of nonabelian derived functors by levelwise using the HKR theorem for this “filtration.”

Definition 2.1.4.11.

We define

F𝖧𝖪𝖱n𝖧𝖧(−/ℤ):𝖠𝗇𝗂(𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀)→𝒟(ℤ)≥0

as the geometric realization preserving extension of τ≥n𝖧𝖧(−/ℤ) from 𝖯𝗈𝗅𝗒.

We see that there is a cofiber sequence

F𝖧𝖪𝖱n⁢𝖧𝖧⁢(R/ℤ)→F𝖧𝖪𝖱n⁢(R/ℤ)→L⁢ΩR/ℤn⁢[n]

for any animated ring R.

Lemma 2.1.4.12.

The nonabelian derived functor F𝖧𝖪𝖱n(−/ℤ) lands in 𝒟⁢(ℤ)≥n. More precisely, for any animated ring R, we have

F𝖧𝖪𝖱n⁢𝖧𝖧⁢(R/ℤ)∈𝒟⁢(ℤ)≥n.
Proof.

The lemma clearly holds for polynomial rings, and the extension to everything else follows from the fact that 𝒟⁢(ℤ)≥n is closed under filtered colimits. □

Lemma 2.1.4.13.

If a functor F:𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀→𝖠𝖻 commutes with reflexive coequalizers, then

H0⁢(L⁢F⁢(R))=F⁡(R).
Proof.

We resolve R by a simplicial diagram of polynomial rings as

and note that R is the reflexive coequalizer of

Therefore, L⁢F⁢(R) is the total complex of

so taking H0, we obtain the reflexive coequalizer of

□

Exercise 2.1.4.14.

Show that the following functors commute with reflexive coequalizers:

  1. 1.

    The functor 𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀→𝖲𝖾𝗍 given by R↦R×n;

  2. 2.

    The functor 𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀→𝖠𝖻 given by R↦ℤ⁡[R×n];

  3. 3.

    The functor Ω−/ℤi:𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀→𝖠𝖻. Hint: think about the generators and relations presentation for ΩR/ℤ1.

We are now ready to give an enhanced version of Theorem 2.1.1.9.

Theorem 2.1.4.15.

If L⁢ΩR/ℤn is concentrated in degree 0 for each n, then Theorem 2.1.1.9 holds for R.

Proof.

Using the long exact sequence in homology associated to

F𝖧𝖪𝖱n+1→F𝖧𝖪𝖱n→L⁢ΩR/ℤn⁢[n],

This implies that

Hn⁢(F𝖧𝖪𝖱n)→H0⁢(L⁢ΩR/ℤn)=ΩR/ℤn

is an isomorphism and that for all i>n, the induced map

Hi⁢(F𝖧𝖪𝖱n+1)→Hi⁢(F𝖧𝖪𝖱n)

is an isomorphism. Descending to R0, we obtain

ΩR/ℤn≃Hn⁢F𝖧𝖪𝖱n≃Hn⁢F𝖧𝖪𝖱0=𝖧𝖧n⁢(R/ℤ).

We will omit checking that this is compatible with multiplication, and that in fact it is the map we had before. □

To better understand this, we need to better understand L⁢ΩR/ℤn. This will in fact agree with the value on R of the nonabelian derived functor

𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀/R)→𝒟⁢(R)≥0→𝒟⁢(ℤ)≥0

which is given by

A↦R⊗AΩA/ℤn

for A∈𝖯𝗈𝗅𝗒/R. By definition, we have

R⊗AΩA/ℤn≃ΛRn⁢(R⊗AΩA/ℤ1).
Exercise 2.1.4.16.

Check that A↦R⊗AΩA/k1 takes compact projective objects in k−𝖠𝗅𝗀/R to compact projective objects in 𝖬𝗈𝖽R.

Applying nonabelian derived functors, we obtain

L⁢ΩR/ℤn=L⁢ΛRn⁢(L⁢ΩR/ℤ1).
Proposition 2.1.4.17.

If L⁢ΩR/ℤ1 is concentraded in degree 0 and ΩR/ℤ1 is a flat R-module, then L⁢ΩR/ℤn is also concentrated in degree 0.

Proof.

If ΩR/ℤ1 is projective, then

L⁢ΛRn⁢(ΩR/ℤ1)=ΛRn⁢(ΩR/ℤ1).

In the general case, we use Lazard’s theorem, which states that every flat R-module is a filtered colimit of finitely generated projective modules. □

We are now able to state the correct form of Theorem 2.1.1.9.

Theorem 2.1.4.18 (Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg, ultimate version).

If L⁢ΩR/k1 is concentrated in degree 0 and ΩR/ℤ1 is a flat R-module, then

𝖧𝖧n⁢(R/ℤ)=ΩR/ℤn.
Remark 2.1.4.19.

For simplicity, we worked over ℤ, but everything still holds if we replace ℤ be an arbitrary commutative ring k.

2.1.5 Hochschild homology of schemes

Let k be a commutative ring and X be a scheme over k. We could in principle allow the base to be non-affine, but for simplicity we will ignore this. There are two approaches:

  1. 1.

    Extending from the affine case (by a right Kan extension);

  2. 2.

    Generalize the functor 𝖧𝖧(−/k) to k-linear dg categories (or stable ∞-categories) and then define define

    𝖧𝖧⁡(X/k)=𝖧𝖧⁡(𝖯𝖾𝗋𝖿⁡(X)/k).

    This is essentially an approach in the spirit of non-commutative geometry and is actually better in many cases (for example, we see that Hochschild homology is really an invariant of a stable ∞-category), but we will take the first approach in these notes since it is closer to the case of rings.

Definition 2.1.5.1.

For a scheme X, we define its Hochschild homology by

𝖧𝖧⁡(X/k)=limU⊆XU⁢ affine open𝖧𝖧⁡(𝒪⁡(U)/k)∈𝒟⁡(k).

Note that if X=Spec⁡R is affine, then

𝖧𝖧⁡(Spec⁡(R)/k) =limU⊆Spec⁡R𝖧𝖧⁡(𝒪⁡(U),k)
=𝖧𝖧⁡(𝒪⁡(Spec⁡R)/k)
=𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)

because U=Spec⁡R is terminal in the poset of affine open subsets of Spec⁡R.

Remark 2.1.5.2.

We can also define Hochschild homology for stacks. For simplicity, we will not do this.

We will now discuss an example of a non-affine scheme. Let X=ℙk1. It has an open cover by

(𝔸k1)+=Spec⁡k⁡[x]and(𝔸k1)−=Spec⁡k⁡[y],

whose intersection is given by

(𝔸k1)+∩(𝔸k1)−=𝔾m=Spec⁡k⁡[x±].

We will hope for some kind of descent of Mayer-Vietoric sequence.

Theorem 2.1.5.3.

For any pair of open subsets U,V⊆X such that X=U∪V, the square

is a pullback in 𝒟⁡(k). In other words, Hochschild homology satisfies Zariski descent.

Remark 2.1.5.4.

Later, we will see that 𝖧𝖧(−/k) satisfies fpqc descent.

Corollary 2.1.5.5.

There is a long exact sequence
Lemma 2.1.5.6.

For any commutative ring R and x∈R, we have

𝖧𝖧⁡(R⁡[x−1]/k)≅𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)⊗RR⁡[x−1].
Exercise 2.1.5.7.

Prove this.

In the example of ℙ1, we have a pullback

This becomes the long exact sequence

Therefore, it is easy to compute

𝖧𝖧1⁢(ℙ1/k)=0,𝖧𝖧0⁢(ℙ1/k)=k⊕k,and𝖧𝖧−1⁢(ℙ1/k)=0.
Proof of Theorem 2.1.5.3.

We always have the square

For any open set U⊂X, a cofinality argument gives

𝖧𝖧⁡(U)=limA⊆X𝖧𝖧⁡(A∩U).

Therefore, without loss of generality that X is affine. Unfortunately, affine schemes can have non-affine open subsets, but another cofinality argument allows us to assume that U and V are affine and are standard opens. Therefore, we have reduced to the case of

where 1∈(x,y). Using the fact that Hochschild homology commutes with localization, this becomes

Therefore, it suffices to prove that

which is a standard fact. This is true because

R⁡[x−1]/R≅R⁡[x−1,y−1]/R⁡[y−1],

which is true because y acts invertibly on R⁡[x−1]/R. This is true because x is invertible on R/y. □

Our goal now is to prove an analog of Theorem 2.1.4.15 and Theorem 2.1.4.18 for schemes. We begin by defining a filtration on 𝖧𝖧⁡(X/k) by the formula

F𝖧𝖪𝖱n⁢𝖧𝖧⁢(X/k)=limU⊆Xaffine openF𝖧𝖪𝖱n⁢(𝖧𝖧⁡(𝒪⁡(U)/k)).
Remark 2.1.5.8.

Note that this cannot be done using the non-commutative approach.

Proposition 2.1.5.9.

This defines a complete filtration on 𝖧𝖧⁡(X/k), namely that

lim→n⁡F𝖧𝖪𝖱n⁢𝖧𝖧⁢(X/k)=0.

Moreover, the associated graded is given by

limU⊆XL⁢ΩU/kn⁢[n]=R⁢Γ⁢(X,L⁢ΩX/kn)⁢[n],

which is usually called the derived Hodge cohomology of X.

Note that if X is smooth, we just get the usual Hodge cohomology.

Proof.

Completeness follows from the fact that it is true for affines and that inverse limits commute with inverse limits. The assertion about (derived) Hodge cohomology follows again from the fact that cofibers commute with limits. □

Using the proposition, we obtain a spectral sequence

R⁢Γ⁢(X,L⁢ΩX/kn⁢[n])⟹𝖧𝖧∗⁢(X/k).
Corollary 2.1.5.10.

If ℚ⊆k, then there is a canonical isomorphism

𝖧𝖧⁡(X/k)≅∏R⁢Γ⁢(X,L⁢ΩX/kn⁢[n]).
Proof.

This is clearly true if X=Spec⁡k⁡[x1,…,xn]. Using non-abelian derived functors, this is also true for any affine X. The general case follows. □

Remark 2.1.5.11.

This isomorphism is in fact compatible with the B operator, so we get the desired results for periodic and negative cyclic homology.

2.2 Topological Hochschild and cyclic homology

2.2.1 Hochschild homology in ∞-categories

Hochschild homology can be constructed in an arbitrary symmetric monoidal ∞-category.

Recall that 𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗ is a 1-category with objects being finite sets and morphisms being maps of finite sets with a linear order on each preimage. Also recall that composition is given by the lexicographic order and that this category is symmetric monoidal with respect to the disjoint union.

In 𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗, the object ⟨1⟩ is an associative algebra object, which means it comes with a multiplication map

⟨1⟩⊔⟨1⟩→⟨1⟩

given by the left copy of ⟨1⟩ being smallest. The unit is the unique morphism from the empty set, and it is clear that multiplication is associative and unital. Therefore, we should think of 𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗ as a kind of free symmetric monoidal category on one associative algebra object, so as before, we define an associative algebra in an ∞-category 𝒞 to be a symmetric monoidal functor

N⁡(𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗)→𝒞.

Of course, the underlying object is simply the image of ⟨1⟩.

Exercise 2.2.1.1.

Prove that the category of symmetric monoidal functors 𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗→𝖠𝖻 is equivalent to the category of rings.

Recall that Hochschild homology was defined by writing a simplicial diagram. However, this is very hard to do by hand in an ∞-category, so we need a systematic way of handling ∞-categories.

Definition 2.2.1.2.

For a finite, nonempty totally ordered set S, define the set of cuts to be

Cut(S)={(S0,S1)|S0,S1⊆S,S0<S1,S0⊔S1=S}.

We form the closely related set of cyclic cuts

Cut𝖼𝗒𝖼⁡(S)=Cut⁡(S)/(S,∅)∼(∅,S).
Exercise 2.2.1.3.

Check that the functor Cut:Δop→𝖲𝖾𝗍 and Cut𝖢𝗒𝖼:Δop→𝖲𝖾𝗍 are represented by the simplicial sets Δ1 and S1.

The functor Cut𝖼𝗒𝖼 actually defines a functor Δop→𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗. For a map f:S→T of totally ordered sets and a cut (S0,S1)∈Cut𝖼𝗒𝖼⁡(S), the preimage

(f∗)−1⁢(S0,S1)⊆Cut𝖼𝗒𝖼⁡(T)

consists of all cuts on T “between” the images f⁡(S0) and f⁡(S1) if the cut is nontrivial. If (S0,S1) is trivial, then the preimage consists of all cuts outside of f⁡(S). To give this an order, in the first case we simply order the cuts from left to right. In the second case, we start with the cuts to the right of f⁡(S) and then go to the cuts to the left of f⁡(S).

Definition 2.2.1.4.

For an algebra A:𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗→𝒞, the Hochschild object is defined by

𝖧𝖧⁡(A/𝒞)≔colimΔop(A∘Cut𝖼𝗒𝖼).
Lemma 2.2.1.5.

For an ordinary ring (or dg algebra), we obtain an algebra A in 𝒟⁡(ℤ). Then there is an equivalence

𝖧𝖧⁡(A/𝒟⁡(ℤ))≃𝖧𝖧⁡(A/ℤ)

between the Hochschild complex of A as an algebra in 𝒟⁡(ℤ) and the Hochschild complex of A defined previously.

Proof.

The functor 𝖢𝗁⁡(ℤ)→𝒟⁡(ℤ) preserves tensor products of K-flat chain complexes. Therefore, if we take our dg algebra to be K-flat, the two sides of the lemma are computing the same object by the fact that in 𝒟⁡(ℤ), a colimit of a simplicial diagram is computed by a total complex. □

Exercise 2.2.1.6.

For an ordinary ring R, prove that the composite

Δop→Cut𝖼𝗒𝖼𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗→𝑅𝖠𝖻

agrees with the cyclic bar complex of R.

Definition 2.2.1.7.

For a ring spectrum A, define its topological Hochschild homology by

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(A)≔𝖧𝖧⁡(A/𝖲𝗉).

Recall that ordinary rings R have Eilenberg-Maclane spectra H⁢R, so we can take their topological Hochschild homology and denote it by 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R).

Example 2.2.1.8.

Because 𝕊 is the unit in 𝖲𝗉, we have 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝕊)=𝕊 for the same reason that 𝖧𝖧∗⁢(ℤ)=ℤ.

This example suggests that we can view 𝖳𝖧𝖧 as 𝖧𝖧(−/𝕊), but it will take some work to make this precise. Before we do this, we will consider things like modules over algebras.

Definition 2.2.1.9.

Define the 1-category 𝖫𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗ in the following way:

  • •

    Objects are finite sets with elements labelled (“colored”) by {a,m};

  • •

    Morphisms are maps S→T together with a total ordering on preimages subject to the conditions that

    • –

      Preimages of a-colored elements are completely a-colored;

    • –

      Preimages of m-colored contain precisely one m-colored element and this element is the maximum.

We can define an analogous category 𝖱𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗ by the same definition, except the m-colored element of a preimage must be the minimum.

Definition 2.2.1.10.

A left module in a symmetric monoidal ∞-category 𝒞 is a symmetric monoidal functor

𝖫𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗→𝒞.

Note that if we only considered a-colored sets, we obtain the underlying algebra of the left module. Now recall that we can tensor left and right modules over a ring R to obtain an abelian group.

Definition 2.2.1.11.

Define a category 𝖫𝖱𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗ by the following:

  • •

    Objects are finite sets with colors given by {r,a,ℓ};

  • •

    Morphisms are maps f:S→T of finite sets with a total ordering on preimages such that

    • –

      Preimages of a-colored elements are entirely a-colored;

    • –

      Preimages of r-colored elements have precisely one r-colored element at the minimum and the rest are a-colored;

    • –

      Preimages of ℓ-colored elements have precisely one ℓ-colored element at the maximum and the rest are a-colored.

Because the r and ℓ-colored elements do not interact, we see that a symmetric monoidal functor 𝖫𝖱𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗→𝒞 is simply a pair of functors 𝖫𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗→𝒞 and 𝖱𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗→𝒞 which agree on 𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗.

Definition 2.2.1.12.

Define the tensor product N⊗AM to be the colimit of the composite

Δop→Cut𝖫𝖱𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗→(N,A,M)𝒞.

Here, the cut functor colors (∅,S) as r, (S,∅) as ℓ, and everything else as a.

There are variants of this theory, including bimodules. In this case, we relax the restriction on preimages of m-colored elements by dropping the condition that it must be either the minimum or maximum. Then Cut𝖼𝗒𝖼 factors through the category 𝖡𝗂𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗ by assigning the color m to the trivial cuts and the color a to everything else. Therefore, if M is a bimodule over A, we have

𝖧𝖧⁡(A/𝒞;M),

which is Hochschild homology of A with coefficients in M.

We can also discuss commutative algebras. Recall that 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗆𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗=𝖥𝗂𝗇, which lets is define commutative algebras in 𝒞.

Lemma 2.2.1.13.

For a commutative algebra A, its Hochschild homology 𝖧𝖧⁡(A/𝒞) has a commutative algebra structure.

We will now study 𝖳𝖧𝖧 for ordinary rings. Eilenberg-Maclane spectra extend to a functor

H:𝒟⁡(ℤ)→𝖲𝗉

coming from the Dold-Kan correspondence. It has the property that

π∗⁢(H⁡(C))=H∗⁢(C).

This functor is lax symmetric monoidal and preserves colimits, so we obtain a canonical map

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(H⁢R)→H⁡(𝖧𝖧⁡(R)).

On homotopy groups, we obtain a morphism

𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(H⁢R)→𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R).

The functor H canonically factors through an equivalence

𝒟⁡(ℤ)→𝖬𝗈𝖽⁡(H⁢ℤ),

which is symmetric monoidal. Therefore, we see that

H⁡(𝖧𝖧⁡(R))=𝖧𝖧⁡(H⁢R/𝖬𝗈𝖽⁡(H⁢ℤ))=𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(H⁢R/H⁢ℤ).
Example 2.2.1.14.

If R is a ℚ-algebra, then the map 𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R)→𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R) is an isomorphism. This follows from the fact that

𝕊⊗H⁢ℚ≃H⁢ℤ⊗H⁢ℚ=H⁢ℚ.

This implies that

S⊗H⁢R≃H⁢ℤ⊗H⁢R,

so we obtain

H⁢R⊗𝕊H⁢R≃H⁢R⊗H⁢ℤH⁢R.
Proposition 2.2.1.15.

For an ordinary ring R, the map

𝖳𝖧𝖧i⁢(R)→𝖧𝖧i⁢(R)

is an isomorphism for i≤2 and surjective for i≥3.

Proof.

The fiber of the map

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)→𝖧𝖧⁡(R)

is the geometric realization of a simplicial diagram of the form

The last term is 0 and the other terms are all 2-connective by a study of the effect of 𝕊→H⁢ℤ on homotopy groups. A technical argument (which we will not give here) shows that homotopy groups come from the last term, the suspension of the second-to-last term, the double suspension of the third-to-last term, and so on, so the geometric realization must be 3-connective. □

If we consider the ordinary ring 𝔽p, we see that

𝖳𝖧𝖧2⁢(𝔽p)≅𝖧𝖧2⁢(𝔽p)≅𝔽p

with generator x.

Theorem 2.2.1.16 (Bökstedt).

There is an isomorphism

𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(𝔽p)≅𝔽p⁢[x].

In particular, we have no divided power structure. In addition, the map

𝔽p⁢[x]→𝔽p⁢⟨x⟩

is zero in degree ≥p.

2.2.2 Bökstedt periodicity

We will now study the spectrum 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p).

Theorem 2.2.2.1 (Bökstedt).

As an 𝔼1-algebra over 𝔽p, 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p) is free on one generator of degree 2. More explicitly, we have

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)≃H⁢𝔽p⊗Σ∞⁢Ω⁢S3.

Note that 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p) is actually an 𝔼∞-algebra, but we are forgetting some of the structure in this theorem. Also, note that Ω⁢Σ⁢S2 is the free 𝔼1-algebra on S2, so

𝖬𝖺𝗉𝔼1/H⁢𝔽p⁢(H⁢𝔽p⊗Σ∞⁢Ω⁢S3,R) ≃𝖬𝖺𝗉𝔼1⁢(Ω⁢S3,Ω∞⁢R)
≃𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒮⁢(S2,Ω∞⁢R)
≃𝖬𝖺𝗉𝖲𝗉⁢(Σ∞⁢S2,R)
≃𝖬𝖺𝗉H⁢𝔽p⁢(Σ2⁢H⁢𝔽p,R)

by a chain of adjunctions.

We should first prove that the two versions of Bökstedt’s theorem are equivalent. If we consider the element x∈𝖳𝖧𝖧2⁢(𝔽p), then we obtain a map of 𝔼1-algebras

H⁢𝔽p⊗Σ∞⁢Ω⁢S3→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p).

This map is an equivalence if and only if it is an equivalence on homotopy groups. Finally, note that the homotopy groups of the source are simply

𝔽p⁢[x],

where x has degree 2. This is because

π∗⁢(H⁢𝔽p⊗Σ∞⁢Ω⁢S3) ≃H∗⁢(Ω⁢S3,𝔽p).

Using the Serre spectral sequence, this is 𝔽p in every even degree. Because Ω⁢S3 is an 𝔼1-algebra, we obtain the desired product structure.

Exercise 2.2.2.2.

Prove that π∗⁢(H⁢𝔽p⊗Σ+∞⁢X) agrees with H∗⁢(X,𝔽p) for any space X.

Lemma 2.2.2.3.

We have an equivalence

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)≃R⊗R⊗𝕊RopR.
Sketch of proof.

Write R≃R⊗RR. This becomes

R ≃R⊗RR
≃||.

Therefore, we have

R⊗R⊗𝕊Rop=colimΔopR⊗R⊗𝕊RopR⊗(s+1).

This construction identifies the rightmost and leftmost copies of R, so it gives us exactly the cyclic bar complex of R. □

We would like to apply this description to 𝔽p. First, we need to understand the spectrum

H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p.

This is quite difficult (because the homotopy groups of spheres are extremely difficult), but it does have an interpretation as the homology groups of the Eilenberg-Maclane spectrum H⁢𝔽p, which form the dual Steenrod algebra.

Theorem 2.2.2.4 (Milnor).

As an algebra, we have

π∗⁢(H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p)={𝔽2⁢[ζ1,ζ2,…]|ζi|=2i−1p=2Λ𝔽p⁢(τ0,τ1,…)⊗𝔽p⁢[ξ1,ξ2,…]|τi|=2⁢pi−1,|ξi|=2⁢pi−2p>2.

This is a very large description of the homotopy groups. Fortunately, there is a direct description of the spectrum H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p, which is an 𝔼∞-algebra over 𝔽p.

Lemma 2.2.2.5.

As an 𝔼2-algebra over H⁢𝔽p, H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p is free on one generator of degree 1. More explicitly, there is an equivalence

H⁢𝔽p⊗Σ+∞⁢Ω2⁢S3≃H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p.
Proof of Theorem 2.2.1.16.

Write

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p) ≃H⁢𝔽p⊗H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽pH⁢𝔽p
≃H⁢𝔽p⊗H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊Σ+∞⁢Ω2⁢S3H⁢𝔽p.

The three terms in the tensor products come from the spaces pt and Ω2⁢S3, so we can form a bar construction with Ω2⁢S3 acting on two copies of a point. Therefore, we obtain

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p) ≃H⁢𝔽p⊗Σ+∞⁢𝖡𝖺𝗋⁢(∗,Ω2⁢S3,∗)
≃H⁢𝔽p⊗Σ+∞⁢Ω⁢S3.

Because we formed the bar construction with an 𝔼2-algebra, we still have an 𝔼1-algebra structure. □

Remark 2.2.2.6.

The description of H⁢𝔽p⊗H⁢𝔽p is equivalent to Bökstedt’s theorem. This is because a map A→B of connected H⁢𝔽p-algebras is an equivalence if and only if the map

H⁢𝔽p⊗AH⁢𝔽p→H⁢𝔽p⊗BH⁢𝔽p

is an equivalence. We simply apply this to the map

H⁢𝔽p⊗Σ+∞⁢Ω2⁢S3→H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p,

which is given by specifying an element of π1.

Exercise 2.2.2.7.
  1. 1.

    Let A be a connected H⁢𝔽p-algebra. Prove that a map N→M of connective A-modules is an equivalence if

    H⁢𝔽p⊗AN→H⁢𝔽p⊗AM

    is.

  2. 2.

    Let A→B be a map of connected H⁢𝔽p-algebras with an equivalence

    H⁢𝔽p⊗AH⁢𝔽p→H⁢𝔽p⊗BH⁢𝔽p.

    Prove that H⁢𝔽p⊗AB≃H⁢𝔽p and that A→B is an equivalence.

If p is odd, there are Dyer-Lashof operations

Qi:πn⁢(R)→πn+2⁢(p−1)⁢i⁢(R),β⁢Qi:πn⁢(R)→πn+2⁢(p−1)⁢i−1⁢(R)

for any 𝔼∞-algebra over H⁢𝔽p. For any element of degree n, then

Qn2⁢x=xp.

In addition, we have

Qi⁢x=0

whenever i<n2. Similarly, when i≤n2, we have

β⁢Qi⁢x=0.

These should be viewed as coming from the homology of configuration spaces. On 𝔼2-algebras, we already have Qn2⁢x whenever n is even and Qn+12⁢x, β⁢Qn+12⁢x when n is odd. The first is simply the p-th power, but the existing power operations for odd n are an additional structure on 𝔼2-algebras.

Theorem 2.2.2.8 (Dyer-Lashof, Araki-Kudo).

We have

H∗⁢(Ω2⁢S3,𝔽p)=Λ𝔽p⁢(a,Q1⁢a,Qp⁢Q1⁢a,…)⊗𝔽p⁢[β⁢Q1⁢a,β⁢Qp⁢Q1⁢a,…].

Note that this is very similar to Milnor’s result. All of the elements given by Dyer-Lashof have the same degrees as Milnor’s elements, so we might try to compare them.

Theorem 2.2.2.9 (Steinberger).

On π∗⁢(H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p), we have

τi=Qpi−1⁢Qpi−2⁢…⁢Q1⁢τ0

and

ξi=β⁢Qpi−1⁢Qpi−2⁢⋯⁢Q1⁢τ0.

Now it remains to try to construct a map realizing our desired isomorphism on homotopy groups.

Proof of Lemma 2.2.2.5.

We have a map

π1⁢(H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p)→π1⁢(H⁢𝔽p⊗H⁢ℤH⁢𝔽p).

The target is simply Tor1ℤ⁡(𝔽p,𝔽p)≃𝔽p. This map is actually an isomorphism (because the map 𝕊→H⁢ℤ is 1-connected). Therefore, we obtain a map

H⁢𝔽p⊗Σ+∞⁢Ω2⁢S3→H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p

of 𝔼2-algebras over H⁢𝔽p. This is an isomorphism on π1, but both sides are generated in the same way by the 𝔼2 Dyer-Lashof operations, so it is an isomorphism on all homotopy groups. □

Exercise 2.2.2.10.

Prove that π1⁢(H⁢𝔽p⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p)≃𝔽p.

2.2.3 Properties of 𝖳𝖧𝖧

We will now consider formal properties of topological Hochschild homology. These include base change results, universality, and more.

Proposition 2.2.3.1.

The functor 𝖳𝖧𝖧:𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉)→𝖲𝗉 is a (strong) symmetric monoidal functor. In particular, there is a natural equivalence

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(A⊗𝕊B)≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(A)⊗𝕊𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(B).

More generally, the functor

𝖧𝖧(−/𝒞):𝖠𝗅𝗀(𝒞)→𝒞

is symmetric monoidal.

Proof.

Consider the forgetful functor U:𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉)→𝖲𝗉 as an object in the symmetric monoidal category 𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉),𝖲𝗉). This is in fact an algebra object. Then we obtain

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(−)≅𝖧𝖧⁡(U/𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉),𝖲𝗉)).□
Corollary 2.2.3.2.

If R is an 𝔼n-algebra, then 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R) is an 𝔼n−1-algebra.

Proof.

Recall that

𝖠𝗅𝗀𝔼n⁢(𝖲𝗉)≅𝖠𝗅𝗀𝔼n−1⁢(𝖠𝗅𝗀𝔼1⁢(𝖲𝗉)).

Applying 𝖳𝖧𝖧 and using the fact that it depends only on the underlying 𝔼1-algebra structure, we land in 𝖠𝗅𝗀𝔼n−1⁢(𝖲𝗉). □

In particular, if R is an 𝔼∞-algebra, so is 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R). However, there is a more canonical description. First recall that if A,B∈𝖢𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉), then A⊗𝕊B is the coproduct in 𝖢𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉).

Proposition 2.2.3.3.

For R∈𝖢𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉), we have

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)≅colimS1R≕R⊗S1,

where we are considering the constant diagram on R.

Exercise 2.2.3.4.

Prove this.

Warning 2.2.3.5.

This colimit is different from the colimit in the category of all spectra, which is given by

colimΔop()≃R⊕Σ⁢R.

We will now prove a base change formula for 𝖳𝖧𝖧.

Proposition 2.2.3.6.

For any lax symmetric monoidal functor F:𝒞→𝒟 and A∈𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝒞), we get a canonical map

𝖧𝖧⁡(F⁢A/𝒟)→F⁡(𝖧𝖧⁡(A/𝒞)).

If F is strong symmetric monoidal and preserves geometric realizations, then this map is an equivalence.

Proof.

We need to compare the cyclic bar constructions

colimΔop()

and

F⁡(colimΔop()).

The latter receives a map from

(colimΔop()),

and this receives a map from the first colimit. The second part follows from the additional assumptions on F. □

Example 2.2.3.7.

Consider the Eilenberg-Maclane functor H:𝒟⁡(ℤ)→𝖲𝗉 which is lax symmetric monoidal. Therefore, we obtain a map

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)→H⁡(𝖧𝖧⁡(R/ℤ))

for any H⁢ℤ-algebra R.

Example 2.2.3.8.

If k→k′ is a map of commutative ring spectra, we have the functor

−⊗kk′:𝖬𝗈𝖽k→𝖬𝗈𝖽k′.

This is symmetric monoidal and preserves all colimits, so we have

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)⊗kk′≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R⊗kk′/k′).

We will now prove a more general version of Bökstedt periodicity. First, recall that an 𝔽p-algebra is perfect if the Frobenius morphism is an isomorphism. Examples include finite fields 𝔽pn and the ring

𝔽p⁢[x1/p∞]=colim(𝔽p⁢[x]→𝜑𝔽p⁢[x]→⋯).

By definition, we have a map

H⁢k→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k)

inducing a map k→𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(k) on homotopy groups. We can then precompose this with a map 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k), so we obtain a map

H⁢k⊗H⁢𝔽p𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k).

On homotopy groups, this gives us a map

k⁡[x]→𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(k).
Theorem 2.2.3.9 (Bökstedt periodicity for perfect rings).

For any perfect 𝔽p-algebra k, the map

k⁡[x]→𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(k)

is an isomorphism of commutative rings. Equivalently, 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k) is the free 𝔼1-algebra on a degree 2 element x over H⁢k.

Proof.

For every perfect ring k, there is a commutative ring spectrum 𝕊W⁡(k) called the spherical Witt vectors such that

𝕊W⁡(k)⊗𝕊H⁢𝔽p≃k.

This should be thought of as a lift of k along 𝕊→H⁢𝔽p. This implies that

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k) ≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝕊W⁡(k)⊗𝕊H⁢Fp)
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝕊W⁡(k))⊗𝕊𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝕊W⁡(k))⊗𝕊𝔽p⊗H⁢𝔽p𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k/H⁢𝔽p)⊗H⁢𝔽p𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)
≃𝖧𝖧⁡(k/𝔽p)⊗H⁢𝔽p𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p).

Therefore, it suffices to prove that

𝖧𝖧∗⁢(k/𝔽p)=0

for all ∗≥1. This is left as an exercise. □

We will conclude with one more base change formula for 𝖳𝖧𝖧. Recall that if k is an 𝔼∞-ring, then 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k)=k⊗S1, so we get a map 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k)→k of 𝔼∞-rings by

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k)=k⊗S1=colimS1k→colimptk=k

along the projection S1→pt. In particular, the composition k→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k)→k is the identity.

Remark 2.2.3.10.

This retract 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k)→k does not exist if k is only 𝔼n for any finite n.

Theorem 2.2.3.11.

If k is a commutative ring spectrum and R is an associative k-algebra, then

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R/k)≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)⊗𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k)k.
Sketch of proof.

We can rewrite

colimΔop()
≃ colimΔop()
≃ colimΔop[()⊗(⋯⁢k⊗𝕊k⇉k)()]
≃ 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)⊗𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k)k.□

2.2.4 The circle action on 𝖳𝖧𝖧

We will now consider the origin of the Connes operator on Hochschild homology from an actual action of §1 on topological Hochschild homology.

Recall that a group action on an object of a 1-category 𝒞 is a functor

B⁢G→𝒞,

where B⁢G is a category with a single object and automorphisms given by G.

Definition 2.2.4.1.

A group action of a group G on an object of a category 𝒞 is a functor

N⁡(B⁢G)→𝒞.

Note that N⁡(B⁢G) is a Kan complex with Ω⁡(N⁡(B⁢G))≃G. This means that the space associated N⁡(B⁢G) is the classifying space of G.

Example 2.2.4.2.

Note that B⁢ℤ≃S1.

Definition 2.2.4.3.

For any grouplike 𝔼1-algebra G in 𝒮 and an ∞-category 𝒞, the category of objects of 𝒞 with G-action is the functor category

𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢G,𝒞).
Definition 2.2.4.4.

Define the homotopy orbits of an object X with G-action as the colimit

Xh⁢G=colimB⁢GX.

Similarly, define the homotopy fixed-points by the limit

Xh⁢G=limB⁢GX.

In the category of spaces, if X has the trivial G-action, then we have

Xh⁢G≃X×B⁢GandXh⁢G≃𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(B⁢G,X).
Exercise 2.2.4.5.

Prove this.

The homotopy orbits should be thought of as a derived version of a quotient construction. For example, if the action of G is free, then we get an actual quotient.

Proposition 2.2.4.6.

Objects in 𝒟⁡(ℤ) with an action of S1 are equivalent to A=Λℤ⁢(ε)-modules in 𝒟⁡(ℤ), where ε has degree 1.

Sketch of proof.

We use the fact that

𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢S1,𝒟⁡(ℤ))≃𝖬𝗈𝖽C∗⁢(S1).

We now need to compare C∗⁢(S1) to its homology A, or more precisely to prove that C∗⁢(S1) is formal. Here, we have maps

These maps are isomorphisms on homology in degrees 0 and 1 and they both factor through τ≤1⁢Free𝔼1⁢(ε). Because τ≤1 is lax symmetric monoidal on 𝒟⁢(ℤ)≥0, we are done. □

Remark 2.2.4.7.

This equivalence is not compatible with monoidal structures on both sides. It does not give the correct answer ∞-categorically when we consider 𝖧𝖢− and 𝖧𝖯, but it is fine on homology.

Theorem 2.2.4.8.

On 𝖧𝖧⁡(R/𝒞), there is a natural S1-action. More precisely, the Hochschild homology functor refines to a functor

𝖧𝖧:𝖠𝗅𝗀𝔼1⁢(𝒞)→𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢S1,𝒞)

which agrees with the S1-action on 𝖧𝖧⁡(R/ℤ) obtained from the Connes operator.

Definition 2.2.4.9.

The paracyclic category Λ∞ is a 1-category with objects given by totally ordered sets with a ℤ-action which are equivalent to sets of the form 1n⁢ℤ and morphisms given by equivariant order-preserving maps.

There is an S1≃B⁢ℤ-action on Λ∞ given by the map

B⁢ℤ×Λ∞→Λ∞

acting trivially on objects and by the map

ℤ×HomΛ∞⁡(1n⁢ℤ,1m⁢ℤ)→HomΛ∞⁡(1n⁢ℤ,1m⁢ℤ)

given by translation.

Definition 2.2.4.10.

The cyclic category Λ is the 1-category with the same objects as Λ∞ and morphisms given by

HomΛ(1nℤ,1mℤ)=HomΛ∞(1nℤ,1mℤ)/ℤ.
Lemma 2.2.4.11.

We have N⁡(Λ)=N⁢(Λ∞)h⁢S1.

This follows from the fact that the ℤ-action is free.

Lemma 2.2.4.12.

We have an equivalence

𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(N⁡(Λ),𝒞)≃𝖥𝗎𝗇⁢(N⁡(Λ∞),𝒞)h⁢S1.
Proof.

We compute mapping spaces. We need to prove that

𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(𝒟,𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(N⁡(Λ),𝒞))≃𝖬𝖺𝗉⁢(𝒟,𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(N⁡(Λ∞),𝒞))h⁢S1.

If we recall that mapping spaces were the maximal Kan complexes in functor categories, we can apply exponential laws. Therefore, it suffices to show that

𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(N⁡(Λ),𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(𝒟,𝒞))≃𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(N⁡(Λ∞),𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(𝒟,𝒞)),

which is just the definition of the colimit. □

Definition 2.2.4.13.

A cyclic object in 𝒞 is a functor N⁡(Λop)→𝒞. There is a functor Δ→Λ∞ sending [n−1] to the set ℤ×[n−1]≅1n⁢ℤ with the lexicographic order. The underlying object of a cyclic object is defined via the restriction

𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(N⁡(Λop),𝒞)→𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(N⁡(Λ∞op),𝒞)→𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(N⁡(Δop),𝒞).

It is natural to wonder what the geometric realization of a cyclic object is.

Lemma 2.2.4.14.

The diagram

commutes. More precisely, the functor Δ→Λ∞ is cofinal.

Lemma 2.2.4.15.

For a cyclic object X, the object

colimΛ∞opX≃colimΔopX

admits an S1-action.

Proof.

Recall that

𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(N⁡(Λ),𝒞)≃𝖥𝗎𝗇⁢(N⁡(Λ∞),𝒞)h⁢S1.

Taking the colimit, we obtain a functor

𝖥𝗎𝗇⁢(N⁡(Λ∞op),𝒞)h⁢S1→colimh⁢S1𝒞h⁢S1≃𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢S1,𝒞).□
Exercise 2.2.4.16.

For an ∞-category 𝒞 with a trivial G-action, prove that

𝒞h⁢G≃𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢G,𝒞).
Proof of Theorem 2.2.4.8.

We now show that the cyclic bar complex is a cyclic object. Let

𝖢𝗎𝗍ℤ:Λ∞op→𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗

be the functor which sends a totally-ordered set S to the set of ℤ-equivariant cuts, which are just partitions of S of the form

S=⋯⊔S−1⊔S0⊔S1⊔⋯

such that each Si is a fundamental domain for the ℤ-action. We need to consider preimages along morphisms f:S→T in Λ∞. These are simply given by the set of all cuts between f⁡(S0) and f⁡(S1) ordered from left-to-right. The functor 𝖢𝗎𝗍ℤ is ℤ-invariant on morphisms, so it factors through

Λ→𝖠𝗌𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍⊗.

Restricting to Δop, we obtain 𝖢𝗎𝗍𝖼𝗒𝖼. □

Exercise 2.2.4.17.

Prove that 𝖢𝗎𝗍ℤ restricts to 𝖢𝗎𝗍𝖼𝗒𝖼.

2.2.5 𝖳𝖧𝖧 of the integers

In this slight digression, we will compute the topological Hochschild homology of the integers.

Theorem 2.2.5.1 (Bökstedt).

We have an isomorphism

𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(ℤ)={ℤ∗=0ℤ/n∗=2⁢n−10else.

In fact, 𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(ℤ) is the homology of the dg algebra

ℤ⁡[x]⊗Λ⁡(e),

where |x|=2, |e|=1, and the differential is given by ∂x=e and ∂e=0.

Note that we can compute the differentials as

⋯→ℤ⁢x2→2ℤ⁢e⁢x→0ℤ⁢x→1ℤ⁢e→0ℤ→0.
Remark 2.2.5.2.

In fact, as an 𝔼1-algebra over H⁢ℤ, 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ) is the Eilenberg-Maclane functor applied to the above dg algebra.

As a consequence of this, we see that

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ)/p=𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ)⊗H⁢ℤH⁢𝔽p

is isomorphic on homotopy groups to the homology groups of the dg-algebra given by 𝔽p⁢[x]⊗Λ⁡(e) with ∂x=e and ∂e=0.

Exercise 2.2.5.3.

Compute the homology of the dg-algebra 𝔽p⁢[x]⊗Λ⁡(e) with ∂e=x and show that it has a nontrivial ring structure.

Definition 2.2.5.4.

For a ring spectrum R, define the p-completion 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R,ℤp)≔𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)p∧, the rationalization 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R,ℚ)≔𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)ℚ, and the ℚp version 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R,ℚp)≔𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R,ℤp)ℚ.

By definition, we can use the Hasse square

to recover 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R).

Lemma 2.2.5.5.

We have an equivalence

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R,ℤp)≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(Rp∧,ℤp)≃𝖧𝖧⁡(Rp∧/𝖲𝗉p∧).

Moreover, we have

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R,ℚ)≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(Rℚ/H⁢ℚ)≃𝖧𝖧⁡(Rℚ/ℚ).
Proof.

First, we note that

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R,ℤp) =(colimΔop())p∧
≃(colimΔop())p∧
≃(colimΔop())p∧
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(Rp∧,ℤp).

The second statement follows for a similar reason. We calculate

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R,ℚ) =𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)⊗𝕊H⁢ℚ
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R⊗𝕊H⁢ℚ/H⁢ℚ)
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(Rℚ/H⁢ℚ).□

As an example, we see that 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ,ℚ)=𝖧𝖧⁡(ℚ/ℚ)=H⁢ℚ. We then turn our attention to 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ,ℤp).

Theorem 2.2.5.6.

We have

𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(ℤ,ℤp)≃{ℤp∗=0ℤp/n⁢ℤp∗=2⁢n−10else.

This is the homology of the the dg-algebra ℤp⁢[x]⊗Λ⁡(e) with the differential ∂x=e.

Proof of Theorem 2.2.5.1 assuming Theorem 2.2.5.6.

Using Theorem 2.2.5.6, we get that 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ,ℚp)=H⁢ℚp. Therefore the fracture square takes the form

It is easy to see now that 𝖳𝖧𝖧0⁢(ℤ)=ℤ and

𝖳𝖧𝖧2⁢n−1⁢(ℤ) =∏p𝖳𝖧𝖧2⁢n−1⁢(ℤ,ℤp)
=∏pℤp/n⁢ℤp
=ℤ/n⁢ℤ

whenever n is nonzero. □

Definition 2.2.5.7.

We define an 𝔼∞-ring spectrum

𝕊⁡[z]≔𝕊⁡[ℕ]=Σ+∞⁢ℕ.

To give a discrete commutative ring R the structure of an 𝕊⁡[z]-algebra is equivalent to giving an element π∈R (so we spend z→π). This is because any map 𝕊⁡[z]→H⁢R factors through H⁢ℤ⁢[x]. We will now consider ℤ as an 𝕊⁡[z]-algebra by sending z to p.

Warning 2.2.5.8.

If we consider a commutative ring spectrum R instead of a discrete ring, then an 𝔼∞-map 𝕊⁡[z]→R is not the same as an element z∈π0⁢R, or in other words 𝕊⁡[z] is not the free 𝔼∞ algebra on a single generator. However, it is free as an 𝔼1-algebra.

Theorem 2.2.5.9 (Relative Bökstedt periodicity).

We have

𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(ℤ/𝕊⁡[z],ℤp)≃ℤp⁢[x].

This has appeared in the work of Lurie, Bhatt-Morrow-Scholze, Antieau-Mathew-Nikolaus, and Krause-Nikolaus.

Proof.

We first note that

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ/𝕊⁡[z],ℤp)/p ≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ/𝕊⁡[z],ℤp)⊗H⁢ℤH⁢𝔽p.
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ/𝕊⁡[z],ℤp)⊗𝕊⁡[z]𝕊
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ⊗𝕊⁡[z]𝕊/𝕊,ℤp)
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p,ℤp)
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p).

Now we study the long exact sequence

and deduce that the homotopy groups 𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(ℤ/𝕊⁡[z],ℤp) are p-torsion-free and concentrated in even degrees. Therefore, there exists an element x∈𝖳𝖧𝖧2⁢(ℤ/𝕊⁡[z],ℤp) lifting x∈𝖳𝖧𝖧2⁢(𝔽p). This gives us a map

ℤp⁢[x]→𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(ℤ/𝕊⁡[z],ℤp)

which is an isomorphism after mod-p reduction. Because these groups are p-torsion-free and p-complete, so this map is an isomorphism on the nose. □

Exercise 2.2.5.10.

Prove that 𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(ℤ/𝕊⁡[z],ℤp) is p-torsion-free and concentrated in even degrees.

Recall that by the base change formula, we have

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R/𝕊⁡[z]) =𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)⊗𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝕊⁡[z])𝕊⁡[z]
=𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)⊗H⁢ℤ⊗𝕊𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝕊⁡[z])(H⁢ℤ⊗𝕊⁡[z])
≃𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)⊗𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ⁡[z]/ℤ)ℤ⁡[z].

We can now consider the HKR filtration on 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(ℤ⁡[z]/ℤ), which induces a filtration on 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R) and thus a multiplicative spectral sequence.

Proposition 2.2.5.11.

There is a convergent, multiplicative spectral sequence

𝖳𝖧𝖧n⁢(R/𝕊⁡[z])⊗ℤ⁡[z]Ωℤ⁡[z]/ℤm⟹𝖳𝖧𝖧n+m⁢(R).

Note that by definition, we have an equivalence

𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/𝕊⁡[z])⊗ℤ⁡[z]Ωℤ⁡[z]/ℤ∗≃𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R/𝕊⁡[z])⊗ℤΛ⁡(dz).

In addition, there is a similar spectral sequence in the p-complete world.

Proof of Theorem 2.2.5.6.

The spectral sequence takes the form

ℤp⁢[x]⊗ℤpΛ⁡(dz)⟹𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(ℤ,ℤp).

Using homological Serre grading, the only differentials are d2.

By the Leibniz rule, it is determined by

d2⁢(x)=α⋅dz∈ℤp⋅dz.

We see that 𝖳𝖧𝖧1⁢(ℤ,ℤp)=ℤp/α⁢ℤp. However, this is equal to

𝖧𝖧1⁢(ℤ/ℤ;ℤp)=0,

so α is a unit in ℤp. Up to changing x by a unit, we may assume that ∂x=dz. Because each degree has a single contribution, there are no extension problems. □

2.2.6 Negative topological cyclic homology

Definition 2.2.6.1.

We define negative topological cyclic homology as homotopy fixed points with respect to the S1-action on topological cyclic homology by the formula

𝖳𝖢−⁢(R)≔𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)h⁢S1.

Recall that an ∞-category is stable if it has finite limits and colimits and all pushout squares are also pullback squares.

Lemma 2.2.6.2.

If 𝒞 is stable, there is a unique lift

whoch is exact in both arguments.

In particular, objects in stable ∞-categories have mapping spectra.

Sketch of proof.

In 𝒞, we write

Y≃Ω⁢Σ⁢Y≃Ω2⁢Σ2⁢Y≃⋯,

and therefore we have

𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(X,Y) ≃Ω⁢𝖬𝖺𝗉⁢(X,Σ⁢Y)
≃Ω2⁢𝖬𝖺𝗉⁢(X,Σ2⁢Y)
≃⋯,

which defines a spectrum. □

The proof of the following lemma is left as an exercise to the reader.

Lemma 2.2.6.3.

If I is a small ∞-category, then

  1. 1.

    The functor category 𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(I,𝖲𝗉) is stable;

  2. 2.

    For any such functor, we have

    limIF≃𝗆𝖺𝗉𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(I,𝖲𝗉)⁢(𝕊,F).

We will now compare 𝖳𝖢− to the negative cyclic homology 𝖧𝖢−.

Proposition 2.2.6.4.

We have

𝖧𝖢−⁢(R)≃𝖧𝖧⁢(R)h⁢S1.
Proof.

We will identify 𝒟⁡(ℤ) with 𝖬𝗈𝖽H⁢ℤ. In particular, we have

𝖧𝖧⁢(R)h⁢S1 ≃𝗆𝖺𝗉𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢S1,𝖲𝗉)⁢(𝕊,𝖧𝖧⁡(R))
≃𝗆𝖺𝗉𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢S1,𝖬𝗈𝖽H⁢ℤ)⁢(H⁢ℤ,𝖧𝖧⁡(R))
≃𝗆𝖺𝗉𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢S1,𝒟⁡(ℤ))⁢(ℤ,𝖧𝖧⁡(R))
≃𝖬𝖺𝗉𝖬𝗈𝖽C∗⁢(S1)⁢(ℤ,𝖧𝖧⁡(R))
≃𝖬𝖺𝗉𝖬𝗈𝖽A⁢(ℤ,𝖧𝖧⁡(R))
≃R⁢HomA⁡(ℤ,𝖧𝖧⁡(R))
≃𝖧𝖢−⁢(R).□

Unfortunately, the formality result we used does not behave well with respect to monoidal structures.

Lemma 2.2.6.5.

The functor (−)hS!:𝖥𝗎𝗇(BS1,𝖲𝗉)→𝖲𝗉 is lax symmetric monoidal and the §1-action on 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R) (or 𝖧𝖧⁡(R)) is compatible with the product structure if R is an 𝔼∞-algebra. In particular, there is an 𝔼∞-algebra structure on 𝖳𝖢−⁢(R) (and 𝖧𝖢−⁢(R)) if R is an 𝔼∞-algebra.

If we want to do calculations, it would be helpful to understand how to compute with homotopy fixed points.

Lemma 2.2.6.6.

Let B⁢S1→𝖲𝗉 be an S1-action on H⁢A for an abelian group A. Then we have

π∗⁢(H⁢A)h⁢S1=A⁡[t]

with t of degree −2.

Proof.

The full subcategory of spectra on all Eilenberg-Maclane spectra (in degree 0) is a 1-category. In particular, we simply have

𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(A,B)≃Hom⁡(A,B)

where we put the discrete topology on Hom⁡(A,B). Therefore, a functor B⁢S1→𝖲𝗉 which takes the basepoint to H⁢A is actually constant. Now we are looking for homotopy fixed points for a constant action, so they are given by

H⁢Ah⁢S1≃𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(Σ+∞⁢B⁢S1,H⁢A).

This has homotopy groups given by H∗⁢(B⁢S1,A), which gives the desired result. □

Exercise 2.2.6.7.

For a spectrum X, prove that

Xh⁢S1≃𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(Σ+∞⁢B⁢S1,X).

For a general spectrum, we can decompose it into its Postnikov tower. Unfortunately, we lose track of extension problems, but there is at least a spectral sequence.

Theorem 2.2.6.8 (Homotopy fixed points spectral sequence).

There is a multiplicative, conditionally convergent spectral sequence

π∗⁢(X)⁢[t]⟹π∗⁢(Xh⁢S1).

Using negative Serre grading, this spectral sequence lives completely in the second quadrant and looks like the below.

Sketch of proof.

We consider the Whitehead tower

⋯⁢τ≥2⁢X→τ≥1⁢X→τ≥0⁢X→⋯

Applying homotopy fixed points, we obtain a sequence

⋯→(τ≥1⁢X)h⁢S1→(τ≥0⁢X)h⁢S1→⋯

which is not the same as taking the Whitehead tower of the homotopy fixed points. The homotopy cofibers are simply Eilenberg-Maclane spectra, so after taking homotopy fixed points they become of the form (H⁢πi⁢X)h⁢S1. Therefore we obtain a filtration on Xh⁢S1, which yields a spectral sequence. □

An S1-action on X gives us a map Σ+∞⁢S1⊗X→X. This uses the fact that S1 is a monoid in spaces, so Σ+∞⁢S1 is a ring spectrum. The canonical map

Σ+∞⁢S1→Σ+∞⁢pt≃𝕊

splits, so we have a decomposition

Σ+∞⁢S1 ≃𝕊⊕Σ∞⁢S1
≃𝕊⊕𝕊1.

Restricting the action to the second summand, we obtain a map

Σ⁢X≃𝕊1⊗X→X,

or in other words a map

b:πn⁢(X)→πn+1⁢(X).
Lemma 2.2.6.9.

In the homotopy fixed points spectral sequence, the differential d2 is determined by the formula

d2⁢α=b⁢α⋅t

for any α∈π∗⁢(X) and d2⁢t=η⁢t2.

Our goal is now to calculate 𝖳𝖢−⁢(𝔽p). The 𝔼2-page of the spectral sequence looks like

and therefore the spectral sequence degenerates at the 𝔼2-page. Therefore, 𝖳𝖢2⁢k−⁢(𝔽p) are complete filtered groups with associated graded a sequence of 𝔽ps.

Now choose lifts t~∈𝖳𝖢−2− and x~∈𝖳𝖢2− which lift t and x, respectively. Then 𝖳𝖢0−⁢(𝔽p)↠𝔽p is surjective and the kernel is generated as an ideal by t~⁢x~. Therefore, we have a relation

p=a⋅t~⁢x~.

In order to compute a, we have a map, recall that we have a map

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)→𝖧𝖧⁡(𝔽p)

which is an isomorphism on τ≤2. Therefore we have an equivalence

(τ≤2⁢𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(𝔽p))h⁢S1→(τ≤2⁢𝖧𝖧⁢(𝔽p))h⁢S1.

The spectral sequence for 𝖧𝖢− showed that t~⁢x~=p, and thus a is a unit. Therefore, we may assume that a=1, so t~⁢x~=p, so we obtain a map

ℤp⁢[t~,x~]/(p−t~⁢x~)→𝖳𝖢∗−⁢(𝔽p).
Theorem 2.2.6.10.

This map is an isomorphism.

Corollary 2.2.6.11.

We have

𝖳𝖢−2⁢k⁢(𝔽p)≃ℤp

and is generated by x~k when k≥0 and t~−k when k≤0.

2.2.7 Topological periodic homology

We will now define a topological version of periodic homology. As a warning, this is not defined by inverting something and may not even be periodic.

Definition 2.2.7.1.

Define the topological periodic homology of a ring spectrum R as Tate fixed points by

𝖳𝖯⁡(R)≔𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)t⁢S1.

Because taking Tate fixed points is lax symmetric monoidal in a way that is compatible with taking homotopy fixed points, we see that 𝖳𝖯⁡(R) is a 𝖳𝖢−⁢(R)-algebra if R is commutative. The homotopy groups of this spectrum can be computed using a spectral sequence.

Proposition 2.2.7.2.

For a spectrum X with G-action, there is a multiplicative, conditionally convergent spectral sequence

πp⁢((H⁢πq⁢(X))t⁢G)⟹πp+q⁢(Xt⁢G).
Proof sketch.

Consider the Whitehead filtration τ≥⁣∙⁢X on X. Applying Tate fixed points, it does commute with this limit even though it does not commute with limits or colimits in general. □

If we want to use this to calculate anything, we need to understand Tate fixed points of Eilenberg-Maclane spectra with respect to S1-actions. This can also be generalized to cyclic groups, but we will not pursue this direction.

For the spectrum H⁢ℤ, we can consider the cofiber sequence

Σ⁢H⁢ℤh⁢S1≃(𝕊adS1⊗H⁢ℤ)h⁢S1→H⁢ℤh⁢S1→H⁢ℤt⁢S1.

Because the first term has only nonnegative homotopy groups and the second has only nonpositive homotopy groups, we can read off the homotopy groups of the Tate fixed points. In particular, we obtain

π∗⁢(H⁢ℤt⁢S1)={ℤ∗ is even0else.
Lemma 2.2.7.3.

We have the ring structure

π∗⁢H⁢ℤt⁢S1≅ℤ⁡[t±].
Proof.

Consider the Tate spectral sequence for H⁢ℤ⊗Σ+∞⁢S1. Because this has a free action, we have

(H⁢ℤ⊗Σ+∞⁢S1)t⁢S1=0.

The spectral sequence takes the form

and so the only way for the spectral sequence to yield zero is for all maps d2 to be isomorphisms. Using the multiplicative structure, we do not get a ring but instead a module over the Tate construction on H⁢ℤ.

Fix generators xi of π2⁢i⁢H⁢ℤt⁢S1 with x−i=ti. Also fix generators σ0 and σ1 of H∗⁢(S1), so that the generator in degree (2⁢i,j) is xi⋅σj. We then compute

d2⁢(σ0) =±x−1⁢t⋅σ1,

where the sign depends on our previous choices. This implies that

d2⁢(xi⁢σ0)=±xi⋅t⁢σ1=±xi−1⋅σi.

Therefore, up to a sign, we have xi⋅t=xi−1. We may choose the xi such that all signs are positive, but this now determines the ring structure. □

Exercise 2.2.7.4.

Using a similar approach to the one given here, compute π∗⁢(H⁢ℤt⁢Cm) as a ring. Hint: use a free action of Cm on a space with easy homology groups.

Remark 2.2.7.5.

If we run the same argument with H⁢A⊗Σ+∞⁢S1 as an H⁢ℤ-module, then we obtain

π∗⁢H⁢At⁢S1=A⁡[t±].

When A is a ring, this is also true as a ring.

Proposition 2.2.7.6.

If X is an object of 𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢S1,𝖬𝗈𝖽H⁢ℤ) (equivalently a module over H⁢ℤ in 𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢S1,𝖲𝗉)), then we have

Xt⁢S1≃Xh⁢S1⊗H⁢ℤh⁢S1H⁢ℤt⁢S1.

In a weaker form, on homotopy groups we have

π∗⁢Xt⁢S1≃π∗⁢Xh⁢S1⁢[t−1].
Sketch of proof.

We have an expression

H⁢ℤt⁢S1≃colim(H⁢ℤt⁢S1→𝑡Σ2⁢H⁢ℤt⁢S1→𝑡⋯)

as H⁢ℤh⁢S1-modules. Therefore, we need to prove that Xt⁢S1 is the same kind of colimit, or in other words that

Xt⁢S1≃colim(Xt⁢S1→𝑡Σ2⁢Xt⁢S1→𝑡⋯).

This clearly works when X is an Eilenberg-Maclane spectrum. Both sides are compatible with fiber sequences, which gives us the case when X has finitely many nonzero homotopy groups. To extend to arbitrary X, we need some connectivity arguments, which we will omit here. □

Exercise 2.2.7.7.

Prove that

H⁢ℤt⁢S1≃colim(H⁢ℤt⁢S1→𝑡Σ2⁢H⁢ℤt⁢S1→𝑡⋯)

as H⁢ℤh⁢S1-modules.

Given that we are calling 𝖳𝖯 topological periodic homology, we would like to see how it is related to the usual periodic homology.

Proposition 2.2.7.8.

We have

𝖧𝖯⁡(R)=𝖧𝖧⁢(R)t⁢S1.
Proof.

Because 𝖧𝖧⁡(R) is an H⁢ℤ-module, we see that 𝖧𝖧⁢(R)t⁢S1 is obtained from 𝖧𝖧⁢(R)h⁢S1=𝖧𝖢−⁢(R) by inverting t. This is exactly how we defined periodic cyclic homology. □

We will now return to topological periodic homology.

Proposition 2.2.7.9.

The Tate spectral sequence for Tate fixed points of S1-actions takes the form

π∗⁢(X)⁢[t±]⟹π∗⁢(Xt⁢S1).

Applying this to topological Hochschild homology gives us a spectral sequence

𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(R)⁢[t±]⟹𝖳𝖯∗⁢(R).

We are now ready to apply it to compute 𝖳𝖯⁡(𝔽p).

Theorem 2.2.7.10.

We have

𝖳𝖯∗⁢(𝔽p)=ℤp⁢[t±].
Proof.

Note that the Tate spectral sequence is simply a periodized of the homotopy fixed points spectral sequence, at least on the 𝔼2-page. Therefore, it degenerates at the 𝔼2-page. The spectral sequence looks like
