and therefore we have just periodized all of the extension problems. Using the map from 𝖳𝖢−, we see that

π−2⁢k⁢𝖳𝖯⁢(𝔽p)=π−2⁢k⁢𝖳𝖢−⁢(𝔽p)≃ℤp⁢t~k.

We will also choose a lift t−1~ of t−1. But now we see that

t~⋅t−1~=1(modhigher filtration),

so it must be a unit. But then t~ is invertible and its negative powers t~−k generate π2⁢k⁢(𝖳𝖯⁡(𝔽p)). □

Warning 2.2.7.11.

If the Tate spectral sequence has differentials, then topological periodic homology may not be periodic. There are even examples with infinitely many differentials where 𝖳𝖯 becomes connective.

2.2.8 The cyclotomic structure

There is an additional structure on topological Hochschild homology which does now exist on ordinary Hochschild homology. This is a map

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)t⁢Cp.
Construction 2.2.8.1.

Assume we have a fiber sequence

X→Y→Z

of pointed connected spaces. Because these are bar constructions of group objects, we write it as

B⁢H→B⁢G→B⁢G/H.

Then there is a functor

B⁡(G/H)→𝒮

which sends pt↦B⁢H which classifies B⁢G, i.e. G/H acts on B⁢H such that

(B⁢H)h⁢G/H≃B⁢G.
Exercise 2.2.8.2.

For a normal subgroup H⊆G of a finite group, describe the G/H-action on B⁢H obtained from the fiber sequence

B⁢H→B⁢G→B⁡(G/H).

As a consequence, for any ∞-category 𝒞, we have an equivalence

𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢G,𝒞)≃𝖥𝗎𝗇⁢(B⁢H,𝒞)h⁢G/H.

With some additional work, this implies that the functors

(−)h⁢H,(−)t⁢H:𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢H,𝒞)→𝒞

induce functors

(−)h⁢H,(−)t⁢H:𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢G,𝒞)≃𝖥𝗎𝗇⁢(B⁢H,𝒞)h⁢G/H→𝖥𝗎𝗇⁢(pt,𝒞)h⁢G/H≃𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(B⁢G/H,𝒞).

In particular, this means that for any normal subgroup H⊆G, if X has a G-action, then Xh⁢H and Xt⁢H have residual G/H-actions such that

(Xh⁢H)h⁢G/H≃Xh⁢G.
Example 2.2.8.3.

Let G=𝕋=U⁡(1)=S1 and H=Cp⊆𝕋 be a cyclic group of prime order embedded as p-th roots of unity. For an object X∈𝒞B⁢𝕋, we see that Xh⁢Cp and Xt⁢Cp have residual 𝕋/Cp-actions. We identify 𝕋/Cp≃𝕋 by the map z↦zp.

Definition 2.2.8.4.

A cyclotomic structure on a spectrum X∈𝖲𝗉B⁢S1 is given by maps

φp:X→Xt⁢Cp

which are 𝕋-equivariant for every prime p. We refer to φp as the cyclotomic Frobenius. A cyclotomic spectrum is a spectrum with a 𝕋-action and cyclotomic structure.

The main fact about cyclotomic spectra that we will discuss is the following.

Theorem 2.2.8.5.

For every ring spectrum R, 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R) admits a natural cyclotomic structure.

Remark 2.2.8.6.

The cyclotomic structure on 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R) is induced from the Tate diagonal

Δp:Id→Tp

on spectra. It does not exist for 𝖧𝖧⁡(R/𝒞) where 𝒞 is an arbitrary stable symmetric monoidal ∞-category. In fact, one can prove that on 𝒟⁡(ℤ) there is no natural map

X→(X⊗ℤ⋯⊗ℤX)t⁢Cp.

Therefore, 𝖧𝖧⁡(R/ℤ) does not admit any kind of cyclotomic structure.

We will now construct the cyclotomic structure. We will first give a construction in the case of an 𝔼∞-ring. First, we will need to discuss induction of G-objects. Let 𝒞 be an ∞-category with all small colimits. Then we have a forgetful functor

𝒞B⁢G→𝒞

for any group G.

Proposition 2.2.8.7.

This functor has a left adjoint given by

c∈𝒞↦colimG(𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍c)=c⊗G

with the G-action on G.

Proof.

Note that

𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒞B⁢G⁢(c⊗G,d) ≃𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒞⁢(c⊗G,d)h⁢G
≃𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒮⁢(G,𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒞⁢(c,d))h⁢G
≃𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒞⁢(c,d).□
Example 2.2.8.8.

Suppose that 𝒞=𝖲𝗉 and G is finite. Then

⨁g∈Gc

is the “free” object.

Example 2.2.8.9.

If G=𝕋, the free 𝕋-object is

c⊗𝕋=c⊕c⁡[1].
Example 2.2.8.10.

This is the important example for the construction we want to perform. Let 𝒞=𝖢𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉) and G be a finite group. If R∈𝖢𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉), then

colimG(R)=R⊗⋯⊗R⏟|G|⁢ times=R⊗G.
Proposition 2.2.8.11.

For R∈𝖢𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉), the map

R→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)

exhibits 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R) as the free 𝔼∞-ring with an S1-action under R.

Proof.

By our general formula, the free object is given by

colimS1(R)=R⊗S1.

As discussed previously, this colimit is 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R). We will omit the proof of the property that the S1-action agrees with the one previously constructed. □

Construction 2.2.8.12.

For every R∈𝖢𝖠𝗅𝗀⁡(𝖲𝗉), the map R→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R) is a map of 𝔼∞-rings. The target has an action of 𝕋, so we obtain an induced Cp-action. Therefore, there is a unique extension a Cp-equivariant map

R⊗⋯⊗R⏟p⁢ times→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R).

Taking Tate fixed points, we obtain a map

(R⊗⋯⁢R)t⁢Cp→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)t⁢Cp.

Also recall that the Tate diagonal is a map

R→(R⊗⋯⊗R)t⁢Cp

of 𝔼∞ rings.

Exercise 2.2.8.13.

Check that the map R⊗p→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R) agrees with the inclusion of the degree p part of the cyclic bar complex.

Using the universal property of 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R), we obtain the cyclotomic Frobenius.

Proposition 2.2.8.14.

There is a unique 𝕋-equivariant map

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)t⁢Cp

of 𝔼∞-rings fitting into the diagram

We will now move on to the case when R is only an 𝔼1-algebra. Recall that by definition, we had

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)=colimΔop(R⊗(n+1))≕colim∙∈Δop(𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)∙),

where 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)∙:Λ→𝖲𝗉 is a cyclic object. This can be written as

where R⊗n+1 carries an action of Cn+1. There is another cyclic object (sdp⁡𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R))t⁢Cp given by

and the cyclotomic structure on 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R) arises by taking the levelwise Tate diagonal. The main complication comes from the way of viewing the target as a cyclic object.

Exercise 2.2.8.15.

For an ordinary ring R, explicitly describe a cyclic object whose underlying simplicial object has degree k part (R⊗(k+1)⁢p)Cp.

As a result, we obtain a map

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)→colimΔop((sdp⁡𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R))t⁢Cp)→(colim[n]∈Δop(R⊗(n+1)⁢p))t⁢Cp=𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)t⁢Cp.

2.2.9 The definition of 𝖳𝖢

We are finally ready to define topological cyclic homology. In fact, we will give two equivalent definitions, one of which is useful for theoretical purposes and one of which is useful for calcuations.

Definition 2.2.9.1.

The ∞-category of cyclotomic spectra is the fiber product

In particular, a map (X,φp)→(Y,φp′) is given by the data of

  1. 1.

    A 𝕋-equivariant map f:X→Y;

  2. 2.

    A 𝕋-equivariant homotopy filling the square

    for every prime p.

In the ∞-category of cyclotomic spectra, the mapping spaces are given by the equalizer

In fact, more is true. We will leave the following proposition as an exercise.

Proposition 2.2.9.2.

The ∞-category 𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉 of cyclotomic spectra is a stable ∞-category and the mapping spectra are given by the equalizer

Moreover, 𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉 has all limits and colimits. In addition, 𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉 has a symmetric monoidal structure given by

(X,φp)⊗(Y,φp′)=(X⊗𝕊Y,X⊗𝕊Y→Xt⁢Cp⊗𝕊Yt⁢Cp→(X⊗𝕊Y)t⁢Cp).

In this monoidal structure, a commutative algebra in 𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉 is given by

  1. 1.

    A commutative ring spectrum X∈𝖢𝖠𝗅𝗀⁢(𝖲𝗉)B⁢𝕋 with 𝕋-action;

  2. 2.

    A 𝕋-equivariant map of commutative algebras

    φp:X→Xt⁢Cp

    for all primes p.

In particular, if R is an 𝔼∞-ring, then 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R) is a commutative algebra in 𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉.

Now recall that negative topological cyclic homology was defined by

𝖳𝖢−⁢(R) =𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(R)h⁢S1
=𝖬𝖺𝗉𝖲𝗉B⁢𝕋⁢(𝕊,𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)).

We will now give a similar description for 𝖳𝖢. In order to do this, we need to give 𝕊 the structure of a cyclotomic spectrum.

Example 2.2.9.3.

The sphere spectrum 𝕊 (with the trivial action) is naturally an 𝔼∞ cyclotomic spectrum.

  • •

    The underlying spectrum with 𝕋-action is 𝕊 with the trivial action;

  • •

    For any prime p, the map

    φp:𝕊→𝕊t⁢Cp

    is the unit

    𝕊→𝕊h⁢Cp→𝕊t⁢Cp.
Exercise 2.2.9.4.

Lift the diagram

𝕊→𝕊h⁢Cp→𝕊t⁢Cp

to a diagram of 𝕋-equivariant maps.

Definition 2.2.9.5.

For a ring spectrum R, define the topological cyclic homology 𝖳𝖢⁡(R) as the mapping spectrum

𝖳𝖢⁡(R)≔𝗆𝖺𝗉𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉⁢(𝕊,𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)).

If R is commutative, then this is an 𝔼∞-ring spectrum. As usual, we will denote the homotopy groups by π∗⁢(𝖳𝖢⁡(R))≕𝖳𝖢∗⁢(R).

More generally, for any cyclotomic spectrum X, we write

𝖳𝖢⁡(X)≔𝗆𝖺𝗉𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉⁢(𝕊,X).

This means that 𝖳𝖢⁡(R)=𝖳𝖢⁡(𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)).

We will now explicitly evaluate this formula. We compute

𝖳𝖢⁡(X) ≃𝗆𝖺𝗉𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉⁢(𝕊,X)
≃Eq⁡()
≃Eq⁡()
≃fib⁡(Xh⁢𝕋→φph⁢𝕋−can∏p(Xt⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋),

where φph⁢𝕋:Xh⁢𝕋→(Xt⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋 is the cyclotomic structure and can:Xh⁢𝕋=(Xh⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋→(Xt⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋 is the canonical map. In this calculation, we have used the following theorem.

Theorem 2.2.9.6.

Assume that X is bounded below with 𝕋-action. Then the canonical map

Xt⁢𝕋→(Xt⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋

exhibits the right hand side as the p-completion of the left hand side. Moreover, if X is p-complete, then so is Xt⁢𝕋 (or in other worse the map is an equivalence).

As a result, if X is a cyclotomic spectrum whose underlying spectrum is bounded below, then

φph⁢𝕋:Xh⁢𝕋→(Xt⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋=(Xt⁢𝕋)p∧.

We can assemble all of the φp into a map

φ:Xh⁢𝕋→∏p(Xt⁢𝕋)p∧≕(Xt⁢𝕋)∧.
Corollary 2.2.9.7.

If X∈𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉 is bounded below, then

𝖳𝖢⁡(X) ≃𝖿𝗂𝖻⁡(Xh⁢𝕋→φ−can(Xt⁢𝕋)∧)
≃Eq⁡().

In particular, we have

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(R)≃Eq⁡()

if R is a connective ring spectrum.

We will briefly discuss the non-affine situation. If X is a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme, then we define

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(X)≔limU⊆Xaffine open𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝒪U).

Therefore, we have

𝖳𝖢−⁢(X)≔𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(X)h⁢𝕋=limU⊆Xaffine open𝖳𝖢−⁢(𝒪U)

and

𝖳𝖯⁡(X)≔𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(X)t⁢𝕋=limU⊆Xaffine open𝖳𝖯⁡(𝒪U).

Finally, we define

𝖳𝖢⁡(X) ≔𝖳𝖢⁡(𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(X))
≃limU⊆Xaffine open𝖳𝖢⁡(𝒪U)
≃Eq⁡().
Remark 2.2.9.8.

One can show that for an n-connective X∈𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉 that 𝖳𝖢⁢(X)p∧≕𝖳𝖢⁡(X,ℤp) is (n−1)-connective. In particular, if R is a ring (or connective ring spectrum), then 𝖳𝖢⁡(R,ℤp) is (−1)-connective.

Proof of Theorem 2.2.9.6.

Note that both ((−)t⁢𝕋)p∧ and ((−)t⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋 are exact and commute with the Postnikov tower. Therefore, we can reduce to the case when X=H⁢A. Resolving A by a two-term complex of free groups, we may assume that A is free. Then the Tate cohomology H⁢At⁢Cp is p-torsion and therefore p-complete. This implies that (Xt⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋 is p-complete. If X itself is p-complete, then Xt⁢𝕋 is p-complete.

We now need to prove that (Xt⁢𝕋)p∧≃(Xt⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋. Because both sides are p-complete, we can check this after reducing mod p. Therefore, we can assume that A=⨁𝔽p is an 𝔽p-vector space. We will now carry out the argument in the case when A=𝔽p.

We need to compare the homotopy groups

π∗⁢((H⁢𝔽p)t⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋.

Recall that when p is odd, we have

π∗⁢(H⁢𝔽p)t⁢Cp≃𝔽p⁢[t±]⊗Λ𝔽p⁢(e).

In addition, we have

π∗⁢(H⁢𝔽p)h⁢Cp≃𝔽p⁢[t]⊗Λ𝔽p⁢(e).

We will now use the homotopy fixed points spectral sequence to compute π∗⁢((H⁢𝔽pt⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋).

The spectral sequence for ((H⁢𝔽p)t⁢Cp)h⁢𝕋=H⁢𝔽ph⁢𝕋 is simply

𝔽p⁢[t]⊗Λ𝔽p⁢(e)⊗𝔽p⁢[x]⟹𝔽p⁢[t].

It is given by

We see that 1 survives. However, 𝔽p⁢[t] is even, so e must be killed and thus d2⁢(e)=x. Applying the Leibniz rule, we obtain more differentials, which give us 𝔽p⁢[t]. The Tate spectral sequence is similar, except we need to invert t. It looks like

There is a map of spectral sequences from the homotopy fixed points spectral sequence to the Tate spectral sequence, so we can import differentials. Therefore, we see that d2⁢(e)=x, d2⁢(t)=0, and d2⁢(x)=0. Therefore, the spectral sequence converges to 𝔽p⁢[t±]. Because there are no convergence problems, we are done. □

Corollary 2.2.10.7.
  • •

    There is an 𝔼∞-map H⁢ℤ→𝖳𝖢⁡(𝔽p);

  • •

Proof.

The first claim follows from the fact that the connective cover is a map H⁢ℤp→𝖳𝖢⁡(𝔽p) and the second claim follows from the fact that 𝖳𝖢⁡(A) is a module over 𝖳𝖢⁡(𝔽p). □

We have an adjunction

We have a map of 𝔼∞-rings

In the relative case, we have that for any 𝔽p-algebra A, 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(A) is naturally an H⁢ℤtr-module.

We will restate the theorem about being an H⁢ℤtr-module in a more algebraic way.

Definition 2.2.10.13.

We define the ∞-category 𝖢𝗒𝖼⁢𝒟⁢(ℤ) of cyclotomic chain complexes as the fiber product

The following characterization of 𝖢𝗒𝖼⁢𝒟⁢(ℤ) is left as an exercise.

Proposition 2.2.10.14.

We have an equivalence

𝖢𝗒𝖼⁢𝒟⁢(ℤ)≃𝖬𝗈𝖽H⁢ℤtr⁢(𝖢𝗒𝖼𝖲𝗉).
Corollary 2.2.10.15.

For an 𝔽p-algebra A, 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(A) is naturally an object of 𝖢𝗒𝖼⁢𝒟⁢(ℤ).

Warning 2.2.10.16.

(Ordinary) Hochschild homology (of an ordinary ring) cannot be made into a cyclotomic chain complex.

2.2.11 𝖳𝖢 of perfect rings

Our goal is now to generalize the computation of 𝖳𝖢⁡(𝔽p) to any perfect ring of characteristic p. In this generality, we will need to replace ℤp by the Witt vectors. Recall that if k is a perfect 𝔽p-algebra, then

𝖳𝖧𝖧∗⁢(k)=k⁡[x].

Recall that there is a commutative ring W⁡(k) called the p-typical Witt vectors of k which is p-torsion free, p-complete, and has W⁡(k)/p≃k. Moreover, it is uniquely determined by these properties.

Theorem 2.2.11.1.

Let R be any derived p-complete ring. Then the reduction mod p map

Hom𝖢𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀⁡(W⁡(k),R)→Hom𝖢𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀⁡(k,R/p)

is a bijection.

Proof.

If R=lim←⁡R/pn is p-complete, then we use obstruction theory to inductively lift maps through the square-zero extension R/pn+1→R/pn. For more details, see Section A.2.2. If R is derived p-complete, then

R=lim←⁡R⫽pn

as an animated ring. Therefore, as in the first step we can reduce to R⫽p. We conclude by using the fact that R⫽p→R/p is a square-zero extension. □

The following corollary is left as an exercise.

Corollary 2.2.11.2.

We have an equivalence of categories
Corollary 2.2.11.3.

There is a ring isomorphism

F:W⁡(k)→W⁡(k)

called the Witt vector Frobenius such that

F/p:k→k

is the Frobenius.

Proposition 2.2.11.4.

For a perfect 𝔽p-algebra k, we have natural isomorphisms

𝖳𝖢∗−⁢(k)≅W⁡(k)⁢[x,t]/(x⁢t−p)and𝖳𝖯∗⁢(k)≅W⁡(k)⁢[t±].
Remark 2.2.11.5.

Note that W⁡(𝔽p)=ℤp, so this matches our previous computation.

Proof.

Consider the homotopy fixed points spectral sequence for 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(k)h⁢𝕋. This is given by

where all dots are given by k. It now remains to solve the extension problems. There is a map of spectral seqeunces from the homotopy fixed points spectral sequence for 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(𝔽p)h⁢𝕋 induced from 𝔽p→k, so we must have

x⁢t=p∈𝖳𝖢0−⁢(k).

However, x⁢t cannot be a zero divisor because this is true on the spectral sequence, so 𝖳𝖢0−⁢(k) is p-torsion free and p-complete with mod-p reduction k. Therefore, we have

𝖳𝖢0−⁢(k)≅W⁡(k).

The rest follows because the spectral sequences are functorial. Periodizing the spectral sequences, we obtain the result for 𝖳𝖯. □

We will now need to understand the maps

can,φ:𝖳𝖢−⁢(k)→𝖳𝖯⁡(k).

We know that can⁡(x)=p⁢t−1, can⁡(t)=t, and can⁡(r)=r for r∈W⁡(k). We also know that φ⁡(x)=t−1 and φ⁡(t)=p⁢t. It remains to study its effect on W⁡(k).

Remark 2.2.11.6.

For any connective ring spectrum, the map π0⁢can:𝖳𝖢0−⁢(R)→𝖳𝖯0⁢(R) is an isomorphism for degree reasons. Thus we can consider π0⁢φ as an endomorphism of 𝖳𝖢0−⁢(R)=𝖳𝖯0⁢(R). This is one of the beginnings of the theory of prismatic cohomology.

Proposition 2.2.11.7.

The map π0⁢φ:W⁡(k)→W⁡(k) is the Witt vector Frobenius F.

Proof.

Consider the diagram

On π0, this diagram induces the diagram

Our goal is to understand the composite of the bottom row of arrows. We know that the composite

k→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(k)→𝖳𝖧𝖧⁢(k)t⁢Cp→kt⁢Cp

is the 𝔼∞ Frobenius. □

Exercise 2.2.11.8.

Prove that for a commutative ring R, the 𝔼∞ Frobenius R→Rt⁢Cp induces the usual Frobenius morphism R→R/p on π0.

Now we calculate 𝖳𝖢∗⁢(k) using the long exact sequence associated with the fiber sequence

𝖳𝖢⁡(k)→𝖳𝖢−⁢(k)→can−φ𝖳𝖯⁡(k).

The map can−φ:𝖳𝖢∗−⁢(k)→𝖳𝖯∗⁢(k) is given as follows:

  • •

    In degree 2⁢n for n≥0, it is the map

    W⁡(k)⋅xn→W⁡(k)⋅t−nα⁢xn↦(α⁢pn−F⁡(α))⁢t−n;
  • •

    In degree −2⁢n, it is the map

    W⁡(k)⋅tn→W⁡(k)⋅tnα⁢tn↦(α−F⁡(α)⁢pn)⁢tn.
  • •

    In degree 0, it is simply id−F.

Note that these maps are isomorphisms whenever n≠0. We have thus proved the following theorem:

Theorem 2.2.11.9.

For a perfect 𝔽p-algebra k, we have

𝖳𝖢∗⁢(k)={W⁢(k)F=ker⁡(id−F)∗=0W⁢(k)F=coker⁡(id−F)∗=−10otherwise.

This formula can be evaluated in various examples using several facts:

  • •

    There is an isomorphism W⁢(k)F≅W⁡(kφ).

    Corollary 2.2.11.10.

    If k is a field, then 𝖳𝖢0⁢(k)=ℤp.

    Proof.

    Clearly we have kφ=𝔽p. □

  • •

    We have kφ=C0⁢(X,𝔽p) for a profinite space X. This is a version of Stone duality. In fact, X is the underlying topological space of Spec⁡kφ. Equivalently, it is the space of connected components of Spec⁡k.

  • •

    We have

    W⁡(kφ) =W⁡(C0⁢(X,𝔽p))
    =C0⁢(X,ℤp)
    ≅C0⁢(Spec⁡kφ,ℤp)
    ≅C0⁢(Spec⁡k,ℤp).
    Exercise 2.2.11.11.

    Prove the third fact from the second.

    Corollary 2.2.11.12.

    For a perfect 𝔽p-algebra, we obtain

    𝖳𝖢0⁢(k)=C0⁢(Spec⁡k,ℤp)=C0⁢(Spec⁡kφ,ℤp).
  • •

    The degree −1 part 𝖳𝖢−1⁢(k)=W⁢(k)F is p-torsion free and its mod-p reduction is kφ. Thus 𝖳𝖢−1⁢(k) is p-completely free of rank the dimension of kφ, or in other words

    𝖳𝖢−1⁢(k)=(⨁Sℤp)p∧

    where kφ=⨁S𝔽p.

    Corollary 2.2.11.13.

    If kφ=0, for example if k is an algebraically closed field, then 𝖳𝖢−1⁢(k)=0.

    As an example, we see that

    𝖳𝖢∗⁢(𝔽¯p)=H⁢ℤp.
  • •

    Suppose that kφ=𝔽p×⋯×𝔽p is a finite product of copies of 𝔽p. Then kφ is a kφ-module and can be described as

    kφ=V1×⋯×Vi

    for some 𝔽p-vector spaces V1,…,Vi. This implies that

    W⁢(k)F=V~1×⋯×V~i

    as a W⁢(k)F=ℤp×⋯×ℤp-module, where V~k is a p-complete, p-torsion free lift of Vi to ℤp.

2.2.12 Frobenius lifts and group rings

We will now study cyclotomic spectra with Frobenius lifts, i.e. spectra where the Frobenius factors through homotopy fixed points. Some examples are Xtr, but more interesting examples are spherical group rings. In these cases, we will give a more explicit formula for 𝖳𝖢.

Definition 2.2.12.1.

A p-cyclotomic spectrum with Frobenius lift is a p-cyclotomic spectrumm X with a 𝕋-equivariant factorization

X→ψpXh⁢Cp→Xt⁢Cp

of the Frobenius.

Example 2.2.12.2.

By definition, the cyclotomic spectrum Xtr with the trivial action has a Frobenius lift because φp was defined as the composite

X→Xh⁢Cp→Xt⁢Cp.

This can be viewed as the map

𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(Σ+∞⁢pt,X)→𝗆𝖺𝗉⁡(Σ+∞⁢B⁢Cp,X).

If X has a Frobenius lift, the map φ:Xh⁢𝕋→Xt⁢𝕋 factors as

In particular, the map φ−can:Xh⁢𝕋→Xt⁢𝕋 factors as

We may now try to use this formula to study 𝖳𝖢.

In our setting, where X is a p-complete, bounded below, p-cyclotomic spectrum with Frobenius lift, then we have a pullback diagram
Proof sketch.

Recall that 𝖳𝖢 is the homotopy fiber of the map φ−can. Therefore, we have a diagram

so the square on the left is a pullback. The proof that the bottom square is a pullback is omitted. □

Corollary 2.2.12.4.

We have the formula

𝖳𝖢⁡(Xtr)=X⊕(X⊗fib⁡(Σ⁢𝕊h⁢𝕋→tr𝕊)).
Exercise 2.2.12.5.

Prove this.

The spectrum fib⁡(Σ⁢𝕊h⁢𝕋→tr𝕊) is usually called Σ⁢ℂ⁢ℙ−1∞. Here, if we desuspend it, it has cells in even degrees starting in degree −2, hence the name.

We will now turn to the case of spherical group rings. Let G be an 𝔼1-group in 𝒮. Recall that Ω and B give an equivalence between these and pointed connected spaces. We will define the group ring to be the spectrum

𝕊⁡[G]≔Σ+∞⁢G.

In order to understand 𝖳𝖢, we will need to understand 𝖳𝖧𝖧.

Lemma 2.2.12.6.

We have the formula

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝕊⁡[G])=Σ+∞⁢L⁢B⁢G,

where L denotes the free loop space.

Proof.

Because 𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝕊⁡[G]) was defined by the cyclic bar construction, we can pull the suspension out of the colimit and obtain

𝖳𝖧𝖧⁡(𝕊⁡[G])=Σ+∞⁢|𝖡𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗒𝖼⁢(G)|.

We now compare 𝖡𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗒𝖼⁢(G) with the cyclic object 𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(S∙,B⁢G), where Sn is the groupoid given by a cycle on {0,…,n}. Unfortunately, 𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(Sn,B⁢G) is not G×n, so there is no levelwise isomorphism. However, it is equivalent to Gh⁢G×n×n, where G×n acts by conjugation on adjacent factors.

This implies that |Fun⁡(S∙,B⁢G)| is obtained from |𝖡𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗒𝖼⁢(G)| by taking orbits under

||,

where the boundary maps are projections. This is contractible. Now we have

𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(Sn,B⁢G) =𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(|Sn|,B⁢G)
≃𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(S1,B⁢G)
≃L⁢B⁢G.□

A Simplicial rings and cotangent complexes

A.1 Simplicial rings and divided power structures

Definition A.1.0.1.

The category 𝗌𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀 of simplicial commutative rings is defined to be the functor category

𝗌𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀≔𝖥𝗎𝗇⁡(Δop,𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀).

More precisely, this is a diagram

satisfying the usual conditions for face and degeneracy maps.

Theorem A.1.0.2 (Eilenberg-Zilber).

The functor

𝗌𝖠𝖻→𝖢𝗁

sending a simplicial abelian group to the associated chain complex is lax symmetric monoidal with respect to the pointwise tensor product on simplicial abelian groups and the usual tensor product on chain complexes.

This implies that every simplicial commutative ring produces a commutative dg algebra. We will now make this product structure explicit.

Definition A.1.0.3.

An (m,n)-shuffle is a function

(μ,ν):[m+n]→[m]×[n]

satisfying the following conditions:

  • •

    Both μ and ν are surjective and order preserving;

  • •

    The maps μ and ν jump at disjoint positions. For example, consider the case when m=n−2, as in Figure A.1.

    We can see that an (m,n)-shuffle is simply a way to shuffle m red and n blue cards together. There is a unique permutation which takes the configuration having all red cards on top to our given shuffle.

Proposition A.1.0.4.

Let R∈𝗌𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀. Then there is a map Rm⊗Rn→⋅Rm+n given by the formula

x⋅y=∑(μ,ν)sign⁡(μ,ν)⁢sμ⁢(x)⁢sν⁢(y),

where sμ⁢(x) and sν⁢(y) correspond to applying the degeneracies making up μ and ν to obtain elements of Rm+n. This gives R the structure of a strict cdga.

Proof.

We will not go through all of the combinatorics explicitly.

  • •

    To prove associativity, we can express both (x⁢y)⁢z and x⁡(y⁢z) as a sum

    ∑(λ,μ,ν)sign⁡(λ,μ,ν)⁢sλ⁢(x)⁢sμ⁢(y)⁢sν⁢(z).
  • •

    To check commutativity, the fact that R was a simplicial commutative ring means we can exchange the roles of μ and ν up to

    sign⁡(μ,ν)sign⁡(ν,μ)=(−1)m⁢n,

    which is exactly what we desire.

  • •

    A variant of this argument also gives strictness. When we compute x2, the summands corresponding to (μ,ν) and (ν,μ) appear with opposite signs, so we see that x2=0.

  • •

    The differential is given by the alternating sum of the face maps. Applying this to x⋅y will decompose the result into (m−1,n)-shuffles and (m,n−1)-shuffles, which yields the desired result. □

We will now discuss divided power structures. In fact, every simplicial commutative ring will give us one of these.

Proposition A.1.0.5.

Let R∈𝗌𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀 be a simplicial commutative ring. Then there exist maps γk:Rn→Rn⁢k for all n,k≥1 such that

  • •

    We have γ1⁢(x)=x for all x∈R;

  • •

    We also have

    γk⁢(x)⁢γℓ⁢(x)=(k+ℓℓ)⁢γk+ℓ⁢(x)

    for all k,ℓ. This means that we should think that xk=k!⁢γk⁢(x);

  • •

    For all x,y∈Rn, we have

    γk⁢(x+y)=∑i+k=kγi⁢(x)⁢γj⁢(y);
  • •

    Similarly, we have

    γk⁢(x⁢y)=xk⁢γk⁢(y);
  • •

    We have the identity

    γk⁢(γℓ⁢(x))=(k⁢ℓ)!k!⁢(ℓ!)k⁢γk⁢ℓ⁢(x).
Proof.

If x is odd, we define γ1⁢(x)=x and γk⁢(x)=0 for all k≥2. This is fine because x2=0 already. If x is even, we have

xk=∑(μ1,…,μk)sign⁡(μ1,…,μk)⁢sμ1⁢(x)⁢⋯⁢sμk⁢(x).

We can permute the factors μ1,…,μk (all of the signs will become +1), and therefore for all σ∈Σk, (μ1,…,μk) and (μσ⁡(1),…,μσ⁡(k)) give the same summand. Choosing one element from each equivalent class, we obtain an element γk⁢(x) such that xk=k!⁢γk⁢(x).

We will omit checking that the properties are satisfied. □

We now need to make sure that this divided power structure behaves well with respect to the chain differential.

Proposition A.1.0.6.

Let R∈𝗌𝖼𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀 be a simplicial commutative ring. Then

  • •

    If x is even, then dγk⁡(x)=γk−1⁢(x)⋅dx;

  • •

    The maps γk preserve boundaries;

  • •

    The γk give a well-defined divided power structure on H∗⁢(R).

Proof.

Suppose that x is a boundary. Then x=dy for x with di⁢y=0 for all i>0. Define

γk′⁢(y)≔∑(μ1,…,μk)Σk⁢-representativessign⁡(μ1,…,μk)⁢sμ1′⁢(y)⁢⋯⁢sμk′⁢(y).

Here, for maps μi:[k⁢n]→[n], we set μi′:[1+k⁢n]→[1+n] to be the maps given by sticking a 1 in front. Then d0⁢γk′⁢(y)=γk⁢(x) and di⁢γk′⁢(y)=0 for all i>0, and therefore dγk′⁡(y)=γk⁢(x). □

A.2 Cotangent complexes and obstruction theory

A.2.1 Definition of the cotangent complex

Recall that we defined

LΩ−/k1:𝖠𝗇𝗂(k−𝖺𝗅𝗀)→𝒟(ℤ)≥0

as the nonabelian derived functor of

Ω1:k−𝖺𝗅𝗀→𝖠𝖻.
Lemma A.2.1.1.

The following constructions agree:

  1. 1.

    The functor

    LΩ−/k1:𝖠𝗇𝗂(k−𝖺𝗅𝗀)→𝒟(ℤ)≥0

    evaluated on R;

  2. 2.

    The functor

    L⁡(A↦R⊗AΩA/k1):𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(k−𝖺𝗅𝗀/R)→𝒟⁢(R)≥0

    evaluated on R.

Proof.

If we begin with the second construction, we obtain

colimi∈ΔopR⊗AiΩAi/k1 ≃colimi∈Δop(colimj∈ΔopAj)⊗Ai𝕃ΩAi/k1
≃colimi∈Δop(colimj∈Δi⁣/opAj)⊗Ai𝕃ΩAi/k1
≃colimi→j∈(Δop)Δ1Aj⊗Ai𝕃ΩAi/k1
≃colimi∈ΔopΩAi/k1
≃L⁢ΩR/k1.

with Ai polynomial rings. Here, we have used the fact that identity morphisms are cofinal in the arrow category. □

The second functor has better categorical properties than the first. Namely, it commutes with coproducts. By definition, this implies that it preserves all colimits.

Example A.2.1.2.

If R=k⁡[x1,…,xn]/(f1,…,fm) is defined by a regular sequence, then the diagram

is a pushout in 𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(k−𝖺𝗅𝗀/R). The functor L(R⊗∙Ω∙/k1) takes this to

where the top arrow is the Jacobian matrix of f1,…,fm. This is also a pushout in 𝒟⁢(R)≥0, and therefore L⁢ΩR/k1 has as H0 and H1 the cokernel and kernel of the Jacobian matrix.

Definition A.2.1.3.

We will call ΩR/k1 the cotangent complex of R relative to k and denote it by LR/k.

A.2.2 Applications to obstruction theory of rings

Let S be a ring and M be an S-module. We can form a split square-zero extension on the S-module S⊕M where

  • •

    If m1,m2∈M, we have m1⁢m2=0;

  • •

    Elements of s multiply as usual;

  • •

    If s∈S and m∈M, then s⁢m is given by the usual action of s on M.

We would like to understand when there is a lift in the diagram

These lifts correspond to φ-linear derivations R→M, which are simply R-module maps

ΩR/k1→φ∗⁢M.
Proposition A.2.2.1.

There exists a functor

𝒟⁢(S)≥0→𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(k−𝖺𝗅𝗀)/S

which sends a projective module P to the square-zero extension S⊕P. We have equivalences of mapping spaces

𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒟⁢(R)≥0⁢(LR/k,φ∗⁢M)≃Fiber⁡(𝖬𝖺𝗉𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(k−𝖺𝗅𝗀)⁢(R,S⊕M)↓𝖬𝖺𝗉𝖠𝗇𝗂⁡(k−𝖺𝗅𝗀)⁢(R,S)).

which does not even split as a morphism of abelian groups. Note that the condition that I2=0 implies that the R~-action on I factors through R.

It turns out that LR/R~ has H0=0 and

H1=R⊗R~I=I.

There is a tautological morphism

LR/R~→I⁡[1]

of R-modules which induces an isomorphism on H1. This corresponds to a map

δ:R→R⊕I⁡[1]

of animated R~-algebras.

Proposition A.2.2.2.

R~ is the pullback of the diagram

in the category of animated R~-algebras.

We see that (not necessarily split) square-zero extensions R~→R along I correspond to maps

LR/k→I⁡[1].

Maps S→R~ lifting a given S→R correspond to diagrams of the form

which are simply lifts

If we unwrap everything, we see that a lift exists if and only if the map

is nullhomotopic. Furthermore, lifts are in correspondence to choices of nullhomotopies. These form a torsor over π1⁢(𝖬𝖺𝗉⁡(LS/k,I⁡[1])). We therefore see that

  • •

    The possible square-zero extensions R~ are classified by

    π0⁢𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒟⁡(R)⁢(LR/k,I⁡[1]);
  • •

    For a given R~ and S→R, there is an obstruction living in

    π0⁢𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒟⁡(S)⁢(LS/k,I⁡[1]).
  • •

    If lifts do exist, they are parameterized by

    π1⁢𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒟⁡(S)⁢(LS/k,I⁡[1])≃π0⁢𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒟⁡(S)⁢(LS/k,I).
Exercise A.2.2.3.

Let S be a k-algebra. Show that the following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    For every square-zero extension R~→R and every S→R, there is a lift (this is usually called being formally smooth).

  2. 2.

    We have H1⁢(LS/k)=0 and H0⁢(LS/k) is a projective S-module.

We are now ready to apply this machinery.

Theorem A.2.2.4.

If R1 is a perfect 𝔽p-algebra (this means that Frobenius is an automorphism), then there exist flat ℤ/pn-algebras Rn, unique up to isomorphism, with

R1≃Rn⊗ℤ/pn𝔽p.

In particular, we have

Rn−1≅Rn⊗ℤ/pnℤ/pn−1,

so we have a tower

⋯→Rn→Rn−1→⋯

whose lift

R≔limRn

is the unique flat, p-complete ℤp-algebra satisfying

R1≅R⊗ℤp𝔽p.

This theorem tells us that there is a way to escape from the positive characteristic to the mixed characteristic setting under the assumption that R1 is perfect.

We will characterize Rn as a non-split square-zero extension of Rn−1 by R1. This is because if it exists, tensoring

0→ℤ/p→ℤ/pn→ℤ/pn−1→0

with Rn gives us

0→R1→Rn→Rn−1→0.

These extensions are classified by

π0⁢𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒟⁡(Rn−1)⁢(LRn−1/ℤ,R1⁢[1]).

They also need to be compatible with the element of

π0⁢𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒟⁡(ℤ/pn−1)⁢(L(ℤ/pn−1)/ℤ,ℤ/p⁡[1])

classifying ℤ/pn→ℤ/pn−1.

Lemma A.2.2.5.

Isomorphism classes of such Rn form a torsor over

π0⁢𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒟⁡(Rn−1)⁢(LRn−1/ℤ/pn−1,Rn⁢[1])≃π0⁢𝖬𝖺𝗉𝒟⁡(R1)⁢(LR1/𝔽p,R1⁢[1]).
Lemma A.2.2.6.

If R1 is a perfect 𝔽p-algebra, then LR1/𝔽p≃0.

Proof.

For any perfect 𝔽p-algebra A, we will consider the effect of the Frobenius φ:A→A on the contangent complex. This induces the zero morphism on ΩA/𝔽p1 (in particular for polynomial rings). Therefore, if we resolve R1 by polynomial rings, φ acts by 0 on LR1/𝔽p. However, because we assumed that R1 is perfect, it must also act by an isomorphism. The desired result follows immediately. □

Putting together the two lemmas, we see that there is a unique isomorphism class of possible Rn, which proves Theorem A.2.2.4.

Definition A.2.2.7.

The R in Theorem A.2.2.4 is called the Witt vectors of R and denoted by W⁡(R0).

Remark A.2.2.8.

Usually the Witt vectors are given by an explicit construction and exist for any 𝔽p-algebra, not just perfect ones, but we believe this explanation is much more satisfying.

Example A.2.2.9.

Consider the finite field 𝔽pn. The Witt vectors W⁡(𝔽pn) is a ℤp-algebra with

W⁡(𝔽pn)/p≃𝔽pn.

One way to construct this is to consider 𝔽pn=𝔽p⁢[x]/f⁡(x) and take the ring

ℤp⁢[x]/f~⁢(x)

for some lift f~ of f.

1 Not in the technical sense.

2 We will not discuss what this is even though it is very fundamental for working with ∞-categories.

1 Because p is a morphism of spaces and not of groups, p−1⁢G looks more algebraic than it is.
